questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Treatment of cholesteatoma with facial paresis in child is: [AIIMS 93]

options.text: Antibiotics to dry ear and then mastoidectomy

questions.explanation: In CSOM, facial palsy may be due to erosion of fallopian canal by cholesteatoma (which erodes fallopian canal) osteitis, or demineralization. The treatment should be urgent mastoid exploration, with decompression of the facial nerve in the fallopian canal.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Treatment of choice for CSOM with vertigo and facial nerve palsy is: [AI 96]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 90; 6/e, p 80.
The patient is presenting with CSOM and vertigo which means cholesteatoma has led to fistula formation involving semicircular canals which in turn has caused vertigo. So the management is immediate mastoid exploration to remove the cholesteatoma.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Most potential route for transmission of Meningitis from CNS to Inner ear is: [AI-09]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 11, 12; 6/e, p 9, 10; Current, Diagnosis and Treatment in Otorhinology 2/143.
Cochlear aqueduct is a bony canal that connects the cochlea to the intracranial subarachnoid space. Perilymph within the cochlear aqueduct is in direct continuation with the CSF and hence Cochlear Aqueduct is the most important route for meningitis to spread to the inner ear.
Vestibular Aqueduct
Vestibular Aqueduct is also a bony connection between the cerebral subarachnoid space and the inner ear. Vestibular Aqueduct contains the endolymphatic duct which contains the endolymph. The endolymph within the endolymphatic duct does not however communicate freely with the CSF as it forms a closed space and ends in a cul-de-sac. Because the endolymph does not directly communicate with the CSF. Vestibular aqueduct is less important in allowing spread of meningitis from CSF to inner ear than Cochlear Aqueduct.
Hyrtle's Fissure
Hyrtle's Fissure is an embryonic remnant that normally obliterates by 24 weeks. When persistent, Hyrtle's fissure provides a connection from the middle ear to the subarachnoid space. Hyrtle's fissure does not directly communicate the internal ear with CSF and usually obliterates early in life and hence is not an important route of spread of infection from CSF to internal ear.
Endolymphatic Sac
Endolymphatic Sac is a cul-de-sac containing endolymph that does not directly communicate with CSF.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Commonest cause of brain abscess: [PGI June 00]
questions.explanation: 50% brain abscess in adults and 25% brain abscess in children are otogenic in origin. In adults cholesteatoma and in children AOM are the M/C causes.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: True about otogenic brain abscess is are:

options.text: H. influenzae is most common causative organism
C.S.O.M. with lat. sinus thrombosis inturn can cause brain abscess
Temporal lobe abscess is associated with personality changes

questions.answerText: C.S.O.M. with lat. sinus thrombosis inturn can cause brain abscess
questions.explanation:
Ref. Turner 10/e, p 311-312; Dhingra 5/e, p 92-93; 6/e, p 82.
Commonest organisms in otogenic brain abscess include gram-negative (Proteus, E. coli, Pseudomonas) and anaerobic bacteria along with Staphylococcus and Pneumococci.
M/C complication of CSOM = Brain abscess.
Lateral sinus thrombosis is usually preceded by a perisinus abscess, which may lead later on to cerebellar abscess.
Temporal lobe abscess is usually associated with hallucinations, visual field defects, and nominal aphasia, while personality change is not a feature of temporal lobe abscess. (It is a feature of frontal lobe abscess.)

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Patient is having scanty, foul smelling discharge from middle ear, develops fever, headache and neck rigidity. CT of the temporal lobe shows a localized ring enhancing lesion, which of the following is least likely cause of this condition: [AI 2011]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 92-93; 6/e, p 82; Turner 10/e, p 311-312.
Commonest organisms in otogenic brain abscess include gram-negative (Proteus, E. coli, Pseudomonas) and anaerobic bacteria along with Staphylococcus and Pneumococci. H. Influenza infection is a rare cause of otogenic abscess.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Lateral sinus thrombosis is associated with all except: [AP 2008]
questions.explanation: Gradenigo sign is associated with petrositis, not lateral sinus thrombosis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Griesinger's sign is seen in: [TN 03]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 95; 6/e, p 84.
Lateral Sinus Thrombophlebitis
It is inflammation of the walls of sigmoid sinus (lateral sinus) with the formation of thrombus. Complication of acute coalescent mastoiditis or masked mastoiditis.
Aetiology: Chronic SOM with cholesteatoma.
Many signs/tests are associated with lateral sinus thrombophlebitis:
Griesingers sign
Tobey Ayer test (Queckenstedt's test)
Crow beck test
Delta sign
Oedema over the posterior part of mastoid due to thrombosis of mastoid emissary veins
In this test CSF pressure is recorded. Internal jugular vein is pressed on one side & again CSF pressure is measured
Pressure on jugular vein on one side produces engorgement of retinal veins. If there is thrombosed sinus, no such change is seen
Seen in CT in case of lateral sinus thrombosis
If no increase in csf pressure → Means a thrombus is present which prevents - in csf pressure → Lateral sinus thrombosis present
If there is increase in pressure → i.e. no Lateral sinus thrombosis present

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: A child was treated for H. Influenza meningitis for 6 month. Most important investigation to be done before discharging the patient is: [AI 99]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Ghai 6th/ed p 518; Dhingra 5th/ed p 132.
H. Influenza Type Meningitis
"It is frequent in children between the ages of 3 and 12 months. Residual auditory deficit is a common complication." ... Ghai 6th/ed p 518.
Since, residual auditory deficit is a common complication of H. influenza meningitis so audiological test to detect the deficit should be performed before discharging any patient suffering from H. influenza meningitis. In children best test to detect hearing loss is brainstem evoked auditory response.
"Auditory brainstem response is used both as screening test and as a definitive hearing assessment test in children". ... Dhingra 4th/ed p 117.

questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with CSOM and vertigo which means cholesteatoma has led to fistula formation involving semicircular canals which in turn has caused vertigo. So the management is immediate mastoid exploration to remove the cholesteatoma.

External rectus palsy (VI nerve palsy) leading to diplopia
Deep seated ear or retro orbital pain (due to V nerve involvement)

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: A 7-year child presenting with acute otitis media, does not respond to ampicillin. Examination reveals full and bulging tympanic membrane, the treatment of choice is: [AI 98]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5th/ed p 71; 6th/ed p 63.
Child presenting with acute otitis media which is not relieved by antibiotics and bulging tympanic membrane is an indication for myringotomy.
Indications of myringotomy in acute otitis media:
Drum is bulging + acute pain.
Incomplete resolution despite antibiotics when drum remains full with persistent conductive deafness.
Persistent effusion beyond 12 weeks.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with fever and ear ache. On examination there is congested tympanic membrane with slight bulge. The treatment of choice is: [AI 95]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5th/ed p 71; 6th/ed p 63.
Fever + earache + congested and bulging tympanic membrane in a four year old child points towards Acute suppurative otitis media as the diagnosis.
Antibiotics (Penicillin) form the mainstay of treatment of acute otitis media and should be administered in a child with Acute otitis media and once tympanic membrane is bulging, myringotomy should be done. Grommet insertion is not indicated in Acute suppurative otitis media. It may be used in cases of myringotomy for serous or secretory otitis media.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Procedure for serous otitis media is: [AP 2002]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5th/ed p 407; 6th/ed p 65; Scotts Brown 7th/ed vol 1 p. 896 and vol 3 p 3392.
In Children
TOC of serous otitis media → myringotomy + insertion of grommet (ventilation tube) along with adenoidectomy (if features of adenoid hyperplasia are present) or tonsillectomy
In Adults (Scots Brown 7th ed vol 3 pg. 3392)
In case of serous otitis media without nasopharyngeal carcinoma: Myringotomy with ventilation tube insertion is done (In adults ventilation tube improves hearing for a very short term < 1 yr)
If there is nasopharyngeal cancer along with serous otitis media: Then there are two treatment options: (i) Hearing aid (ii) Myringotomy without ventilation tube insertion
Recently, CO2 laser assisted tympanic membrane ventilation has been advocated for the treatment of adult OME.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Grommet tube is used in: [TN 2002]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5th/ed p 71, 73; 6th/ed p 65, 66; Scotts Brown 7th/ed vol/pg 896-897.

Meniere's disease

questions.stem: Ideal site for myringotomy and grommet insertion: [CUPGEE 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5th/ed p 71, 73; 6th/ed p 65, 398; S/B 7/ed Vol, pg 896-897.
For serous otitis media/Grommet insertion, ideal site is anterior inferior quadrant (though Dhingra says it can be posterior inferior also) as is proven by the following lines from scotts brown: Site of insertion of grommet "Insertion of the ventilation tube posterosuperiorly is not recommended because of the potential for damaging the ossicular chain. It makes no difference to the extrusion rate as to whether the tube is inserted through a radial or circumferential incision and whether sited anterosuperiorly rather than antero-inferiorly. Placement antero-inferiorly compared with placement postero-inferiorly lengthens the time a ventilation tube is in situ. To maximise the duration of potential tube function, the preferred insertion site is anteroinferior through a circumferential or radial incision. Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, vol/p 896-897.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Radical mastoidectomy is done for: [DNB 2000]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 337; 6/e, p 317.
Radical mastoidectomy is a procedure to eradicate disease from middle ear and mastoid without any attempt to reconstruct hearing. It is rarely done these days - Its only indications are:
Malignancy of middle ear
When cholesteatoma cannot be removed safely eg if it invades eustachian tube, round window or perilabyrinthine cells
If previous attempts to eradicate cholesteatoma have failed

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: All of the following steps are done in radical mastoidectomy except: [AI 97]

options.text: Removal of middle ear mucosa and muscles
Removal of all ossicles of eustachian tube plate
Maintainance of patency of eustachian tube

questions.answerText: Maintainance of patency of eustachian tube
questions.explanation: In radical mastoidectomy, the Eustachian tube is obliterated by a piece of muscle or cartilage. So maintenance of patency is not done.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Radical mastoidectomy includes all except: [AIIMS 00]
questions.explanation:
Following steps are done in radical mastoidectomy:
Posterior meatal wall is removed and the entire area of middle ear, attic, antrum and mastoid is converted into a single cavity, by removing the bridge and lowering the facial ridge.
All remnants of tympanic membrane, ossicles (except the stapes foot plate) and mucoperiosteal lining are removed (Not cochlea)
Eustachian tube is obliterated by a piece of muscle or cartilage
The diseased middle ear and mastoid are permanently exteriorized for inspection and cleaning.
Remember: Bridge is the most posterosuperior part of bony meatal wall lateral to aditus and antrum, which overlies the Notch of Rivinus while facial ridge lies lateral to fallopian canal. Bridge is removed and ridge is lowered in radical or modified radical operation.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Nerve damaged in radical mastoidectomy is: [MH 2000]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scotts Brown 7/e vol 3 p 3434.
Complications of mastoid surgery - are actually very uncommon:
Facial palsy (rare)
Total hearing loss/dead ear
NOTE
The incidence of facial palsy is widely accepted to be rare in the hands of expert surgeons, however, total loss of hearing also occurs in the hands of expert.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Modified radical mastoidectomy is indicated in all except: [MP 2000]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 411; 6/e, p 400.
Now, this is one of those questions where we can get the answer by exclusion. Here we know - management of coalescent mastoiditis is cortical mastoidectomy so obviously modified radical mastoidectomy is not done in this case.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: A 30-year-old male is having Attic cholesteatoma of left ear with lateral sinus thrombophlebitis. Which of the following will be the operation of choice? [AI 06]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 82; 6/e, p 73; Turner 10/e, p 304; Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 670; 5/e; 7/e Vol 3, p 3432-3433.
As discussed in attic cholesteatoma we do and if cholesteatoma invades eustachian tube or perilabyrinthine tissue then management is Radical Mastoidectomy. Now whether we perform radical mastoidectomy or modified radical mastoidectomy both are canal wall down procedures.

questions.explanation:
Ref. Scotts Brown 7/e, vol-3 p 3436.
CSOM/cholesteatoma generally presents with conductive type of hearing loss. If cholesteatoma (CSOM) is presenting with sensorineural hearing loss, it means it is associated with some complications or it can be due to the use of potentially ototoxic ear drops. Management would still remain Radical mastoidectomy.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: All of the following techniques are used to control bleeding from bone during mastoid surgery except: [AIIMS Nov. 04]

options.text: Cutting drill over the bleeding area
Diamond drill over the bleeding area
Bipolar cautery over the bleeding area

questions.answerText: Cutting drill over the bleeding area
questions.explanation:
Ref. Essential of ENT Mohan Bansal, p 437.
Here the answer is obvious as Cutting drill over the bleeding area will increase the bleeding instead of stopping it.
Diamond drill over the bleeding area will produce heat and stop the bleeding. Bipolar cautery can be used to control bleeding during mastoid surgery (Not monopolar cautery). Bone wax is also commonly used to control bleeding during mastoid surgery (It seals the bleeding site).

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Communication between middle ear and Eustachian tube is obliterated in which surgery: [Delhi 2005]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 403.
In radical mastoidectomy, the opening of Eustachian tube is closed by curtting its mucosa and plugging the opening with tensor tympani muscle or cartilage.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Otitis media with effusion is also known as: [PGI May 2012]
questions.explanation: Dhingra 6/e, p 64. Otitis media with effusion is also called as serous otitis media, secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media and glue ear.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 7: Diseases of Middle Ear
questions.stem: Mr. Ramu presented with persistent ear pain and discharge, retro-orbital pain, modified radical mastoidectomy was done to him. Patient comes back with persistent discharge, what is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 79.
In the question patient is a case of CSOM, with local spread of infection. Dhingra clearly mentions in a patient with CSOM, persistent ear discharge with or without deep seated pain in spite of an adequate cortical or modified mastoidectomy points towards petrositis. Persistent ear discharge with or without deep seated pain in spite of an adequate cortical or modified radical mastoidectomy also points to petrositis.
Petrositis: Important Points
Spread of infection from middle ear and mastoid to the petrous part of temporal bone is petrositis
It can also involve adjacent 5th cranial nerve and 6th cranial nerve when it produces classical triad of symptoms - 6th nerve palsy, retro orbital pain (5th nerve) and persistent discharge from the ear, known as Gradenigo's syndrome
Note: All the three classical components of Gradenigo's syndrome are not needed for diagnosing petrositis.
Treatment: Adequate drainage is the mainstay of treatment along with specific antibiotic therapy. Modified radical or radical mastoidectomy is often required if not done already. The fistulous tract should be identified, curetted and enlarged to provide free drainage.
END OF CHAPTER 7 MCQs
This completes Chapter 7 (Diseases of Middle Ear) with all MCQs, explanations, and relevant theory content integrated. The chapter now covers:

Cholesteatoma - Congenital, Primary acquired, Secondary acquired, Theories (Wittmack, Sade, Ruede, Habermann), Levenson criteria
Complications of Otitis Media - Extracranial (Mastoiditis, Petrositis/Gradenigo, Facial paralysis, Labyrinthitis, Osteomyelitis, Bezold/Citelli/Luc/Zygomatic abscess) and Intracranial (Meningitis, Extradural/Subdural abscess, Brain abscess, Lateral sinus thrombophlebitis, Otitic hydrocephalus)
Acute Mastoiditis - Stages, Abscess types, Treatment
Petrositis/Gradenigo's Syndrome - 3D triad (Discharge, Diplopia, Deep orbital pain)
Lateral Sinus Thrombophlebitis - Griesinger sign, Tobey-Ayer test, Crow-Beck test, Delta sign
Brain Abscess - Temporal lobe (M/C), Cerebellar, Clinical features, Ring sign on CT
Surgical Management - Myringotomy, Myringoplasty, Tympanoplasty (Types I-V), Cortical/Simple/Schwartz Mastoidectomy, Radical Mastoidectomy, Modified Radical Mastoidectomy
Landmarks - MacEwen's triangle, Citelli's angle, Trautmann's triangle, Donaldson's line

questions.stem: The Sensorineural hearing loss in Meniere's disease is characterized by:

options.text: Both high and low frequencies affected simultaneously

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, page 101. Initially hearing loss in Meniere's disease affects lower frequencies later involves higher frequencies also. This is because in Meniere's, there is accumulation of endolymph which starts from the apex of cochlea (scala media), thus affecting the lower frequencies initially.
Frequency localization of Cochlea: Higher frequencies are localized in the basal turn and lower ones in the apex. Ref. TB of ENT, Tuli 2/e, p 115.

G - Glue ear

P - Perilymph fistula (labyrinthine fistula)

questions.stem: Diagnostic test for Meniere's disease:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 101. Electrocochleography is the diagnostic test for Meniere's disease. Normally, ratio of summating action potential to action potential (AP) is 30%. In Meniere disease SP/AP is greater than 30%.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: Which of the following is not a typical feature of Meniere's disease? [AIIMS May 06]
questions.explanation: Pulsatile tinnitus is seen in glomus jugulare, AV shunts, aneurysms, stenotic arterial lesions. It may also occur in secretory otitis media. In the early stages of disease most patients are well in between the attack. As the disease progresses patients may have persistent hearing loss, tinnitus and postural imbalance between the attacks of vertigo. Some patients in the later stages develop drop attacks k/a Tumarkin or otolithic crisis due to otolith dysfunction. During this attack patient simply drops without a warning. There is no associated vertigo or loss of consciousness.

questions.stem: All are manifestations of Meniere's disease except: [AII 97]

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: Meniere's disease is characterized by: [AII 04]

options.text: Vertigo ear discharge tinnitus and headache
Vertigo, tinnitus hearing loss and headache

questions.answerText: Vertigo, tinnitus hearing loss and headache
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 112; 6/e, p 100, 101; Tuli 1/e, p 127; Harrison 17/e, p 202; Turner 10/e, p 335.
Meniere's Disease is Characterised by:
Episodic vertigo (accompanied by nausea vomiting and vagal disturbances like abdominal cramps, diarrhea and bradycardia)
Fluctuating deafness of sensorineural type
Fluctuating tinnitus
Aural fullness
Emotional disturbances, headache and anxiety.
NOTE
Pulsatile tinnitus is seen in glomus jugulare, AV shunts, aneurysms, stenotic arterial lesions. It may also occur in secretory otitis media. In the early stages of disease most patients are well in between the attack. As the disease progresses patients may have persistent hearing loss, tinnitus and postural imbalance between the attacks of vertigo. Some patients in the later stages develop drop attacks k/a Tumarkin or otolithic crisis due to otolith dysfunction. During this attack patient simply drops without a warning. There is no associated vertigo or loss of consciousness.

questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 111; 6/e, p 103. Dilatation of endolymphatic sac is seen in Meniere's disease and also in acoustic neuroma.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: Meniere's disease is: [PGI June 99]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 111; 6/e, p 103. Meniere's disease, which is an idiopathic lesion, is a clinical diagnosis. The following conditions, which are included in Meniere's syndrome or secondary Meniere's disease, can mimic the clinical features of Meniere's disease and should be kept in mind:
Migraine and basilar migraine
Autoimmune disease of inner ear and otosclerosis
Syphilis and Cogan's syndrome
Cardiogenic
Vertebral basilar insufficiency
Trauma: Head injury or ear surgery
Acoustic neuroma
Also Know
Lermoyez syndrome is a variant of Meniere's disease, where initially there is deafness and tinnitus, vertigo appears later when deafness improves.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: True about Endolymphatic hydrops: [PGI June 06]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 112; 6/e, p 100-101.
Meniere's disease lead to sensorineural hearing loss and not conductive type. Generally unilateral. Age = Most common 35-60 years. It is more common in males.
Also remember:
Otosclerosis - Bilateral condition, more common in females
Bell's palsy - Unilateral condition with equal sex distribution
Acoustic neuroma - Unilateral condition with equal sex distribution
Glomus tumor - More common in females

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: Glycerol test is done in: [AP 1995, TN 2000]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 113; 6/e, p 102. Glycerol is a dehydrating agent. When given orally, it reduces endolymph pressure and causes improvement in hearing as evidenced by an improvement of 10 dB or 10% gain in discrimination score in Meniere's disease patients.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: In a classical case of Meniere's disease which one of the following statement is true: [Karn 01]

options.text: Carhart's Notch is a characteristic feature in pure tone audiogram
Schwartz's sign is usually present in the tympanic membrane
Low frequency sensorineural deafness is often seen in pure tone audiogram
Decompression fallopian canal is the treatment of choice

questions.answerText: Low frequency sensorineural deafness is often seen in pure tone audiogram
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 113; 6/e, p 101; Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 98-99; 6/e, p 87; Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 116; 6/e, p 104.
Carhart's notch and Schwartz's sign are seen in otosclerosis.
Decompression of endolymphatic sac (and not fallopian canal) is done in Meniere's disease. Decompression of Fallopian canal is done in traumatic facial nerve palsy.
Meniere's disease is associated with - SNHL which affects low frequencies first, followed by higher frequencies later. This is visible on pure tone audiogram.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: Recruitment phenomenon is seen in: [DNB 2007/Kolkata 2002]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 31, 113; 6/e, p 101.
Recruitment Phenomenon
It is a phenomenon of abnormal growth of loudness
The ear which does not hear low intensity sound begins to hear greater intensity sounds as loud or even louder than normal hearing ear. Thus a loud sound which is tolerable in normal ear may grow to abnormal levels of loudness in the recruiting ear and thus become intolerable
Recruitment is typically seen in lesions of cochlea i.e. Meniere's disease, presbycusis.
Patients with recruitment are poor candidates for hearing aids.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: Vasodilators in Menieres disease are useful because they: [Kerala 94]
questions.explanation: Ischaemia of endolymphatic sac → ↓ absorption of endolymph → Endolymphatic hydrops/Meniere's disease. Vasodilators improve labyrinthine circulation, so increase endolymph reabsorption.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)

During chronic attack: Nicotinic acid, Betahistine

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: A 55-year-old female presents with tinnitus, dizziness and h/o progressive deafness, which of the following is not a D/D: [AIIMS 2001]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 616.
Delayed Endolymphatic Hydrops
Hydrops sometimes develop in patients who have lost their hearing in one or both ears previously. The causes of hearing loss vary, from head injury, meningitis or any other etiology. Patient subsequently develops attacks of vertigo similar to that seen in Meniere's disease in a delayed fashion.
Histiocytosis X belong to the group of disorders collectively termed inflammatory reticuloendotheliosis characterized by multiple osteolytic lesions involving skull, temporal bone, long bones, ribs, and vertebrae. There is generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and in severe cases involvement of the bone marrow. Involvement of temporal bone leads to features mimicking complicated like otorrhea, mastoiditis, facial palsy, and labyrinthitis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: Initial mechanism of action of intra-tympanic gentamicin microwick catheter inserted into inner ear in treatment of Meniere's disease: [AIIMS Nov. 2012]

options.text: Binds to hair cell Na+-K+ ATPase channel
Acts on melanoreceptors of outer hair cell

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 116; 6/e, p 104.
Intratympanic Gentamicin Therapy
Gentamicin is mainly vestibulotoxic. It has been used in daily or biweekly injection into the middle ear. Drug is absorbed through round window and causes destruction of vestibular labyrinth. Total control of vertigo spells has been reported in 60-80% of patients with some relief from symptoms in others. Hearing loss, sometimes severe and profound, has been reported in 4 to 30% of patients treated with mode of therapy.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 8: Meniere's Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
questions.stem: Which of the following is true about Meniere's disease? [AIIMS Nov. 2014]

options.text: Surgery is the mainstay of treatment
Electrocochleography is the gold standard investigation for diagnosis
Sement's maneuver is used for treatment
In initial stages, inverted 'V' shaped audiogram is seen

questions.answerText: Electrocochleography is the gold standard investigation for diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 100-104; 5/e, p 112-113; Logan-Turner 10/e, p 335.
"Electrocochleography is the gold standard investigation for diagnosis in Meniere's disease."
Electrocochleography is diagnostic in Meniere's disease. Ratio of Summating Potential (SP) to Action Potential (AP) is greater than 30%.
Initial management of meniere's disease is medical management and not surgery.
In initial stages: An upsloping audiogram is seen, as lower frequencies are affected earlier. Later when higher frequencies are also affected, then a flat audiogram is seen.
END OF CHAPTER 8 MCQs
This completes Chapter 8 (Meniere's Disease/Endolymphatic Hydrops) with all MCQs, explanations, and relevant theory content integrated. The chapter now covers:
Definition - Triad of episodic vertigo, fluctuating deafness, fluctuating tinnitus + aural fullness
Incidence - Males > females, Age 35-60 years, Unilateral
Pathology - Distension of endolymphatic system (cochlear duct/scala media and saccule)
Pathophysiology - Disturbance in production or absorption of endolymph
Clinical Features - Vertigo, Fluctuating hearing loss, Diplacusis, Tinnitus, Aural fullness, Tullio's phenomenon, Hennebert's sign, Drop crisis (Tumarkin)
Investigations - Tuning fork tests, PTA (low frequency SNHL initially), Speech audiometry, BERA, Electrocochleography (SP/AP > 30%), Caloric tests, Glycerol test, Reverse glycerol test
AAO-HNS Classification - Certain, Definite, Probable, Possible
Variants - Cochlear hydrops, Vestibular hydrops, Lermoyez syndrome
Treatment - Medical (Vestibular sedatives, Vasodilators, Diuretics, Meniett device), Labyrinthine exercises (Cooksey-Cawthorne), Surgical (Conservative - Intratympanic gentamicin, Endolymphatic sac decompression, Shunt operation, Sacculotomy; Destructive - Labyrinthectomy, Vestibular nerve section)
Secondary Endolymphatic Hydrops - D/D of Meniere's disease
continue

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Neurofibromatosis type 2 is associated with:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Current Otolaryngology 3/e p 801, 802.
B/L acoustic neuromas are a hallmark of Neurofibromatosis 2.
Neurofibromatosis Type 2 is an autosomal dominant. Gene for NF-2 is located on chromosome 22q.
Patients with NF2 present in second and third decade of life, rarely after the age of 60.
M/C symptom/Presenting symptom = Hearing loss.
Skin tumors are present in nearly two thirds of patients of NF-2.
Cafe au lait spots, which are a hallmark of NF-1, are also frequently found in patients with NF2. In contrast to patients with NF1, patients with NF2 invariably have fewer than six of these hyperpigmented lesions. Juvenile posterior subcapsular lenticular opacities are common and have been reported in up to 51% of patients with NF 2. Ref. Current Otolaryngology 3/e, p 801, 802.
So as is clear from above lines - cafe au lait spots and posterior subcapsular lenticular opacity are seen in NF-2 also.
Remember: Diagnostic criteria for NF-2
I. Bilateral Acoustic neuromaorII. Family history of NF-2 and U/L Vestibular schwannoma/acoustic neuromaorIII. Any two of the following:
Meningioma
Glioma
Neurofibroma
Schwannoma
Posterior subcapsular lenticular opacity
NOTE: In patients of Neurofibromatosis-2 operated for B/L acoustic neuroma, best method of hearing rehabilitation is - auditory brainstem implant.

Ref. Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 765; 3/e, p 791-92; Turner 10/e, p 39; Dhingra 5/e, p 124; Dhingra 6/e, p 112.
Points to Remember
M/C CP angle tumour is Acoustic neuroma = 80%
2nd M/C CP angle tumor is meningioma ≈ 10%

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: Cerebellopontine angle tumor produces: [PGI 2005]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Current otolaryngology 3/e p 792.
The two most common CP angle tumors are:
Acoustic neuromas
Meningiomas
M/C symptom = U/L Deafness2nd M/C symptom = TinnitusM/C nerve involved = Facial nerve → Therefore absent corneal reflex is seen.
In meningiomas: Unlike Acoustic neuroma - Trigeminal neuralgias, facial paresis, lower cranial nerve deficits and visual disturbances are more common.
Hence all the above features are seen in CP angle tumors.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma

questions.stem: Acoustic neuroma commonly arise from: [AI 11, AI 10, AIIMS Nov. 09; AIIMS Dec. 98, Jand K - 05]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Logan Turner 10/e, p 339; Ref. Glasscock-Shambaugh, Surgery of the Ear, 6/e, p 644.
Historically, the superior vestibular nerve sheath was thought to be the site of origin, giving rise to nearly two-thirds of tumors. More recent reviews show the inferior vestibular nerve to be the predominant site of origin for these tumors.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma

questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5th/ed pg 124, 6th/ed p 112. The first extracanalicular nerve to be involved is trigeminal (CN V).

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: Earliest sign seen in Acoustic neuroma is: [UPSC 05]
questions.explanation:
Feature
Details
Most common nerve from which vestibular schwannoma arises
Inferior vestibular nerve
Earliest symptom
Progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss often accompanied by tinnitus
Earliest cranial nerve to be involved by acoustic neuroma
VIII nerve followed by V nerve followed by VII nerve
Earliest presentation of Vth nerve involvement/Earliest sign of Acoustic neuroma
Decreased corneal sensitivity
Significance of Vth nerve involvement
Implies that tumor is at least 2.5 cm in size and occupies cerebellopontine angle
Earliest presentation of VII nerve involvement
Involvement of Sensory fibers leading to hypoesthesia of posterior meatal wall (Hitzelberger sign)
NOTE: Although facial nerve is involved, facial nerve palsy is rarely seen.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: Acoustic neuroma causes: [PGI June 99]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Tuli 1/e, p 114.
SNHL can be:a. Cochlear SNHL: Hair cells are mainly damaged.b. Retrocochlear SNHL: There is lesion of VIIIth nerve or its central connections.
Acoustic neuroma cause retrocochlear type of SNHL as it damages VIIIth nerve.
Meniere's disease causes cochlear deafness.
NOTE: Important features of Retro Cochlear hearing loss/Acoustic Neuroma:
Sensorineural hearing loss more marked in high frequencies.
Poor discrimination score (0-30%)
Recruitment phenomenon absent and roll over phenomenon present i.e. discrimination score further decreases when loudness is increased beyond a particular point.
Short increment sensitivity index (SISI) test will show a score of 0-20% in 70-90% cases.
Tone decay significant.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: Hitzelberger's sign is seen in: [AI 08]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 124, 6/e, p 112. Hitzelberger's sign is hypoesthesia of posterior meatal wall seen in vestibular Schwannoma/acoustic neuroma due to involvement of sensory fibres of VIIIth nerve.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: In acoustic neuroma all are seen except: [MP 2000]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott's Brown 7/e, vol-3 p 3959; Dhingra 5/e, p, 124-125, 6/e, p 112, 113.
In Acoustic Neuroma:
Loss of corneal reflex is seen - due to the involvement of Trigeminal nerve
Tinnitus - due to pressure on cochlear nerve
Large tumors can cause diplopia
Facial palsy is rarely seen because motor fibers of facial nerve are resistant to pressure.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: In a patient with acoustic neuroma all are seen except: [SGPGI 07]

options.text: Facial nerve may be involved unilateral deafness

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 124.
Lets see Each Option Separately:
Option a - Facial nerve may be involved - This is correct as we have discussed in previous Questions, facial nerve may be involved but complete palsy does not occur.
Option b - Reduced corneal reflex - This is correct reduced corneal reflex is the first sign of Trigeminal nerve involvement.
Option c - Cerebellar signs - This is correct.
Option d - Acute episodes of vertigo: "Vestibular symptoms seen in acoustic neuroma are imbalance or unsteadiness. True vertigo is seldom seen" - Dhingra 5/e, p 124, 6/e, p 112. Acute episode of vertigo is a rare presenting feature in acoustic neuroma since it is a slow growing tumor so there is adequate time for compensation.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: Earliest ocular finding in acoustic neuroma: [PGI 00]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 124; Turner 10/e, p 341.
Earliest nerve involved by acoustic neuroma - Vth nerve/trigeminal nerve.
Earliest manifestation of Vth nerve involvement is decreased corneal sensitivity leading to loss of corneal reflex.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: Vestibular neuroma not correct: [AP 2005]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 125.
As far as the answer is concerned - I am sure no one has any doubts about it because corneal reflex is absent in acoustic neuroma.
But lets focus on option c i.e. Absence of caloric response - In acoustic neuroma - Caloric test will show diminished or absent response in 96% patients due to vestibular involvement. Hence option c i.e. correct.
Also Know: Criteria of suspicion for Acoustic neuroma (Turner 10th/ed pg 341)
Unilateral deafness of less than 10 years.
Sudden deafness with retrocochlear involvement which does not respond to steroids.
Poor speech discrimination score in relation to pure tone threshold.
Spontaneous nystagmus with eyes closed on electronystagmography without a history of disequilibrium.
Absence of caloric response in case of normal hearing.
Hearing loss with reduced corneal reflex.
Local pain.
NOTE: If hearing loss is the only symptom and it is of more than 10 years duration, an acoustic neuroma is most unlikely as a tumor which has been growing for longer than this period because it will give features of other cranial nerve or brainstem involvement also.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma

options.text: Upper pole displaces IX, X, XI nerves
Lower pole displaces trigeminal cranial nerve

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 114; 5/e, p 134.
Here Option a i.e. malignant tumor is incorrect as acoustic neuroma is a benign tumor.
Option b: It arises from vestibular nerve is correct.
Option c: Upper pole displaces IX, X and XI nerve - incorrect, as is evident from the diagram given in the text: Upper pole displaces III, IV and V nerve whereas lower pole displaces IX, X and XI nerve.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: A patient is suspected to have vestibular schwannoma the investigation of choice for its diagnosis is: [AIIMS 04]
questions.explanation: Ref. Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 767; Dhingra 5/e, p 126. MRI with gadolinium contrast is the gold standard for the diagnosis or exclusion of vestibular Schwannoma.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 11: Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma
questions.stem: A 70-year-old male presents with loss of sensation in external auditory meatus (Hitselberger sign positive). The likely diagnosis is: [AI 2008]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 112. This is a case of vestibular schwannoma where involvement of sensory fibres of VIIth nerve leads to anesthesia over the posterosuperior part of external meatus and canal. This is known as Hitselberger sign.
END OF CHAPTER 11 MCQs
This completes Chapter 11 (Lesion of Cerebellopontine Angle and Acoustic Neuroma) with all MCQs, explanations, and relevant theory content integrated. The chapter now covers:
Anatomy of IAC - Contents (Facial nerve in anterosuperior, Superior vestibular in posterosuperior, Cochlear in anteroinferior, Inferior vestibular in posteroinferior)
Anatomy of CPA - Boundaries, Contents (AICA, VII, VIII, V, IX, X, XI)
Lesions of CP Angle - Acoustic neuroma (80%), Meningioma (10%), Congenital cholesteatoma (5%), Others (5%)
Vestibular Schwannoma/Acoustic Neuroma - M/C intracranial schwannoma, 80% of CP angle tumors, 10% of brain tumors, Benign, Encapsulated, Slow growing
Site of Origin - Inferior vestibular nerve (M/C) > Superior vestibular nerve > Cochlear nuclei
Neurofibromatosis 2 - B/L acoustic neuroma, Chromosome 22q, Cafe-au-lait spots, Posterior subcapsular lenticular opacity, Diagnostic criteria
Clinical Features - Earliest symptom (Cochleovestibular - deafness, tinnitus), Most common symptom (Progressive U/L SNHL), Hitzelberger's sign, Reduced corneal reflex (earliest sign of V nerve involvement), Facial nerve involvement (sensory fibers early, motor fibers late), Cerebellar signs, Raised ICT
Histopathology - Antoni A (Verocay bodies), Antoni B
Classification - Grade I-V (According to size)
Investigations - Audiological (Retrocochlear hearing loss, Tone decay > 30 dB, Recruitment negative, Roll over phenomenon, BERA - best test), Vestibular (Caloric test - diminished/absent), IOC = Gadolinium enhanced MRI (100% diagnostic yield)
Treatment - Surgery (Retrosigmoidal, Middle cranial fossa, Retrolabyrinthine, Translabyrinthine - M/C approach), Hearing rehabilitation (Cochlear implant, Auditory brainstem implant for B/L acoustic neuroma), Stereotactic radiosurgery/Gamma knife (Co-60), Cyber knife
continue

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear · New-pattern question
questions.stem: M/C benign tumor the external auditory canal is:
questions.explanation: Ref. Essentials of ENT Mohan Bansal p 160. Exostoses are the M/C benign tumor of external auditory canal.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear · New-pattern question
questions.stem: M/C benign tumor of middle ear:
questions.explanation:
Glomus tumor is the M/C benign tumor of middle ear.
Important points on Ear Tumors:
Of all the cases of ear carcinomas - 85% occur on Pinna, 10% in external canal and 5% in middle ear.
M/C benign tumor of external canal - Exostosis.
M/C benign tumor of middle ear - Glomus tumor.
Exostosis are M/C in divers, swimmers and hence also called as surfers ear.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear · New-pattern question
questions.stem: IOC for Glomus tumor:
questions.explanation: See the text for explanation. CT scan is the investigation of choice. Helps to distinguish glomus jugulare from glomus tympanicum.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear · New-pattern question
questions.stem: A 42-year female presents with U/L progressive conductive hearing loss with pulsatile tinnitus and blood stained discharge. She also complains of headache, sweating and palpitations. All of the following investigations are warranted in this case except:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 110.
Remember: A 42-year-old female complaining of U/L conductive hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus points towards Glomus tumor. Otoscopy should be done as it shows characteristic red reflex. Patient is complaining of headache, palpitations, etc. i.e the tumor is secreting catecholamine, so serum catecholamine and urine VMA levels should be measured. Biopsy is contraindicated in Glomus tumors since they are very vascular and can bleed profusely.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear · New-pattern question
questions.stem: FISCH classification is used for:
questions.explanation:
FISCH classification of glomus tumor:
Type
Extent
Management
Type A
Confined to middle ear
Excised through external auditory meatus i.e. transmeatal route
Type B
Extending to mastoid
Excised through combined approach from meatus and mastoid
Type C
Extending to labyrinth and involving petrous apex
Excised through infratemporal fossa approach
Type D
Intracranial extension
Posterior fossa craniotomy

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: The usual location of Glomus jugular tumor is: [Delhi 90, UP-03]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 120, 6/e, p 109.
Glomus tumor is of 2 types:
Glomus jugulare:
Arises from: Dome of jugular bulb, Hypotympanum
Invades: Jugular foramen therefore involves cranial nerves IX to XII and compresses jugular vein
Clinical features: Signs of compression of cranial nerves IX to XII
Glomus tympanicum:
Arises from: Promontory of middle ear
Clinical features: Aural symptoms sometimes with facial paralysis

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: Earliest symptom of glomus tumor is: [UP 06]
questions.explanation:
The two most common presenting symptoms of paraganglioma of temporal bone (Glomus tumor) are conductive hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus.
Hearing loss is conductive and slowly progressive. Tinnitus is pulsatile and of swishing character, synchronous with pulse and can be temporarily stopped by carotid pressure.
Thus, both pulsatile tinnitus and deafness are seen in glomus tumor.
According to Turner 10/e, p 214: The earliest symptom of a glomus tumor is pulsatile tinnitus.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: Pulsatile tinnitus in ear is due to: [TN 01]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 120, 6/e, p 109. Pulsatile tinnitus: Seen in Glomus tumor. Pulsatile otorrhea: Seen in ASOM.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: True about Glomus jugulare tumor: [PGI June 04]

options.text: Pulsatile tinnitus and conductive type of hearing loss seen

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 120, 6/e, p 109-110; Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 794-800, 3/e, p 814, 815, 816.
Glomus tumor is more common in females.
Glomus tumor is also referred to as chemodectoma or nonchromaffin paraganglioma.
Glomus tumor is a benign tumor, therefore lymph node metastasis is not present.
Multicentric tumors are found in 3-10% of sporadic cases and in 25-50% of familial cases.
Fluctuating (Pulsatile) tinnitus and conductive hearing loss are the earliest symptoms of glomus tumor.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: All are true about glomus jugulare tumors except: [UP 03]

options.text: It is a disease of infancy
It invades labyrinth, petrous pyramid and mastoid

questions.answerText: It is a disease of infancy
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 120-121, 6/e, p 109-110.
Let us see each option separately:
Option a - Common in females: It is correct as females are affected five times more than males.
Option b - Causes sensorineural deafness: This is partially correct as glomus tumor leads to mainly conductive type hearing loss. Sensorineural hearing loss is uncommon but can occur if the tumor erodes the dense otic capsule bone and invades the inner ear.
Option c - It is a disease of infancy: This is incorrect as Glomus tumor is seen in middle age (40-50 years).
Option d - It invades labyrinth, petrous pyramid and mastoid: This is correct.
Spread of Glomus tumor:
It can perforate the tympanic membrane
It can spread intracranially to posterior and middle cranial fossa
It can invade labyrinth, petrous pyramid and mastoid
It can invade jugular foramen & base of skull causing IXth to XII nerve palsy
Through Eustachian tube it can spread to nasopharynx

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: Brown sign is seen in: [AI 07]
questions.explanation: Pulsation sign/Brown sign/Blanching sign is positive in Glomus tumor (when ear canal pressure is raised with Siegel's speculum, tumor pulsates vigorously and then blanches; reverse happens with release of pressure).

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: Phelp's sign is seen in: [AIIMS May 02]
questions.explanation:
Phelp's sign, Rising sun sign, Pulsation sign/Brown sign, Aquino sign are all seen in Glomus tumor.
Phelp sign: This sign is seen on CT scan. In CT - in case of glomus jugulare tumor the normal crest between the carotid canal and jugular fossa is absent whereas it is not so in case of glomus tympanicum.
For details of other signs see the preceding text.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: The glomus tumor invasion of jugular bulb is diagnosed by: [UP 05]
questions.explanation:
MRI - gives soft tissue extent of tumor; Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) shows compression of the carotid artery whereas magnetic resonance venography shows invasion of jugular bulb by the tumor.
Remember: Preoperative biopsy is never done in case of glomus tumor as it can lead to bleeding.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: A patient presents with bleeding from the ear pain tinnitus and progressive deafness. On examination, there is a red swelling behind the intact tympanic membrane which blanches on pressure with pneumatic speculum. Management includes all except: [AIIMS Nov. 01]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 121, 6/e, p 110; Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 801, 802.
Patient presenting with progressive deafness, tinnitus and bleeding from ear + Red swelling behind the intact tympanic membrane (i.e. rising sun sign) + Swelling blanches on pressure with pneumatic speculum (i.e. Brown's sign) → Indicate Glomus tumor as the diagnosis.
Management includes: Surgery, Radiotherapy (for inoperable lesions, old age and unfit patients), Preoperative embolization (to decrease vascularity of tumor before surgery). Interferons have no role in Glomus tumor.

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear

questions.stem: Which is the most pulsatile tumor found in external auditory meatus which bleeds on touch: [AIIMS 95]

questions.chapter: Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 12: Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear
questions.stem: Treatment of middle ear malignancy includes: [Mahe 07]

options.text: Excision of petrous part of temporal bone

questions.answerText: Excision of petrous part of temporal bone
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 122-123, 6/e, p 110-111.
Most common malignant tumor of middle ear and mastoid is squamous cell carcinoma.
Clinical Features:
It affects age group 40-60 years
Slightly more common in females
Most important predisposing cause is long standing CSOM
Patient may present with chronic foul smelling blood stained discharge
Pain is severe and comes at night.
Facial palsy may be seen
O/E - Friable, hemorrhagic granulation or polyp are present.
Diagnosis - made only on biopsy. CT and angiography are done to see the extent of disease. Metastasis occurs to cervical lymph nodes later.
Treatment of carcinoma of middle ear is combination of surgery followed by radiotherapy. Surgery consists of radical mastoidectomy/subtotal or total petrosectomy depending on the extent of tumor.
END OF CHAPTER 12 MCQs
This completes Chapter 12 (Glomus Tumor and Other Tumors of the Ear) with all MCQs, explanations, and relevant theory content integrated. The chapter now covers:
Glomus Tumor (Paragangliomas) - M/C benign tumor of middle ear, Chemodectoma, Neural crest origin, Glomus jugulare (dome of jugular bulb) vs Glomus tympanicum (promontory), M/C site in middle ear: Hypotympanum
Features - Slow growing, Locally invasive, Noncapsulated, Highly vascular, Main blood supply: Ascending pharyngeal artery, Middle-aged females (4th-5th decade), Malignant transformation rare, <10% secrete catecholamines
Pathology - Chief cells (Zellballen), Acetylcholine, Catecholamine, Serotonin, Rich vascular plexus, Bilateral in 1-2%, Hereditary, Associated with phakomatoses and MEN Type I
Rule of Ten - 10% familial, 10% secrete catecholamines, 10% multicentric
Spread of Tumor - Tympanic membrane (Vascular polyp), Labyrinth/petrous/pyramid/mastoid (Hearing loss), Jugular foramen/base of skull (CN palsies VII, VIII, IX-XII), Eustachian tube (Mass on nasopharynx), Intracranial, Lung/liver/lymph nodes
M/C cranial nerve involved - Facial nerve followed by last four cranial nerves
Clinical Features - Intratympanic: Earliest symptoms deafness (conductive) and pulsatile tinnitus, Red reflex/Rising sun appearance, Pulsation sign/Brown sign/Blanching sign, Aquino sign; As polyp: Profuse bleeding, Dizziness, Vertigo, Facial paralysis, Earache, Otorrhea, Audible bruit
Pulsatile Tinnitus - Arterial (Glomus tumor, AV malformation, Aberrant ICA, Carotid/subclavian atherosclerosis), Venous (High jugular bulb, Benign ICT)
Investigations - Examination under microscope (Pulsatile mass), Catecholamines levels (Serum catecholamines, Urine VMA), CT scan (IOC - Phelp's sign), HRCT + Gadolinium enhanced MRI, Audiogram, Angiography (Carotid arteriography, Jugular venography, Vertebral arteriography)
Biopsy - Contraindicated (Very vascular)
Treatment - Surgery (Microsurgical total tumor removal), Alpha-blockade with phentolamine for secreting tumors, Embolization (Preoperative to decrease vascularity; Sole treatment in inoperable patients), Radiation (Inoperable, old age, unfit patients)
Complications - Hearing loss (Conductive > SNHL), Hypoglossal nerve palsy, Facial nerve palsy, Ipsilateral Horner syndrome, Jugular foramen syndrome (IX, X, XI)
FISCH Classification - Type A (Middle ear), Type B (Mastoid), Type C (Labyrinth/petrous apex), Type D (Intracranial)
Other Tumors - Exostosis (M/C benign tumor of EAC), Osteoma, Squamous cell carcinoma (M/C malignant tumor of middle ear), Ceruminoma, Sebaceous adenoma, Papilloma, Fibroma
okay

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods · New-pattern question
questions.stem: A 1-year-child with anotia (absence of Pinna) on right side is brought by the parents to ENT clinic with concern of hearing loss on right side. What is the best device in such a case, if hearing loss is confirmed:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 122.
BAHA is primarily suited for people who have unilateral conductive hearing loss as the device is based on bone conduction. In the question, child is having ANOTIA on right side (i.e. absent outer ear) with hearing loss on right side (obviously). In this case cochlear implants cannot be used as they are suitable for B/L hearing loss. BAHA is the best hearing aid in this case. Now comes at what time should it be implanted. At 6 years - surgical reconstruction of pinna is done, but if we wait till that time - child's speech will get affected. Hence it is better to put BAHA device as early as possible.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Following implantation of cochlear implant, activation of the device is done after:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 126. Activation of the cochlear implant is done 3-4 weeks after implantation. Following this, the implant is programmed (called as mapping). Mapping is done on regular basis during postoperative rehabilitation.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods · New-pattern question
questions.stem: All of the following investigations are done before implanting cochlear implant except:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 126.
Preoperative Investigations done before Cochlear Implant Surgery:
For imaging of temporal bone, cochlea, auditory N and brain: CT, MRI
For audiological evaluation: PTA, Tympanometry, Otoacoustic emission, Auditory brainstem response, Auditory steady state response.
Hearing aid trial - speech perception and discrimination score
Speech aid language evaluation
Psychological evaluation
Note: After cochlear implantation has been done, in postoperative period and later also MRI is contraindicated. CT can be done.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: In cochlear implants electrodes are most commonly placed at:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 140, 6/e, p 126. Electrodes are most commonly placed at round window and then passed into scala tympani.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: Cochlear implant is done in: [Bihar 05]
questions.explanation:
M/C Surgical approach for placing cochlea implant = Facial Recess approach (Posterior tympanotomy) which involves doing a cortical mastoidectomy. From the middle ear the electrodes are then introduced into the scala tympani through the round window.
Recently Veria technique (Non-mastoidectomy technique) is gaining popularity for cochlear implantation. It uses transcanal approach.
Advantage of Veria technique
Simple
Less chances of injuring facial nerve
Suitable in young children where mastoid has not developed fully
Minimal bone trauma: fast healing and less complication rate

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: Which of the following statement regarding cochlear implant is true: [AIIMS Nov 10]

options.text: Cochlear malformation is not a CI to its use
Contraindicated in children < 5 yrs of age

questions.answerText: Cochlear malformation is not a CI to its use
questions.explanation:
Ref. Current Otolaryngology 3/e, p 856; Dhingra 5/e, p 139, 140.
Explanation
As discussed earlier Cochlear implants are useful in B/L severe to profound hearing loss and not in mild-moderate hearing loss: Option C is incorrect.
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 125: Cochlear implants can be implanted in children at 12 months of age, rather early implantation gives better results. (Dhingra 5th/ed, p 139), 6th/ed, p 125.
"The timing of implantation is very important. Earlier implantation in children generally yields more favorable results and many centers routinely implant children under 12 months of age." Ref. Current Otolaryngology 3/e, p 856.
So friends - Option b - C/I in children < 5 years of age is incorrect.
Approach for cochlear implants is via facial recess, where a simple cortical mastoidectomy is done first and short process of incus and lateral semicircular canal is identified. The facial recess is operated by performing a posterior tympanotomy. A cochleostomy is then done inferior to round window (Not oval window) with the goal of affording access to scala tympani (where the electrode has to be placed). Thus option d i.e. it is approached through oval window is incorrect.
So by exclusion our answer is a i.e. cochlear malformation is not a contraindication to its use.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: Cochlear implant is done if the following is intact: [AIIMS Nov 12]
questions.explanation:
Ref. TB of Mohan Bansal, Textbook of Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 1/e, p 178.
Cochlear Implants
They are indicated for patients of profound binaural SNHL (with non functional cochlear hair cells) who have intact auditory nerve functions and show little or no benefit from hearing aids." Ref. Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 178.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: Which intervention is best in patients operated for bilateral acoustic neuroma for hearing rehabilitation: [PGI Nov 2012]
questions.explanation:
Auditory brainstem implant (ABI)
This implant is designed to stimulate the cochlear nuclear complex in the brainstem directly by placing the implant in the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle. Such an implant is needed when CN VIII has been severed in surgery of vestibular schwannoma. In these cases, cochlear implants are obviously of no use."
In unilateral acoustic neuroma, auditory brainstem implant (ABI) is not necessary as hearing is possible from the contralateral side but in bilateral acoustic neuroma as in neurofibromatosis-2, rehabilitation is required by ABI. Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 127.
Note: Brainstem implant is currently used only in patients with NF-2 and is always implanted simultaneously with tumor removal (usually during excision of the patient's second tumor). It is useful in patients who have had both cochleovestibular nerves sacrificed, since this implant stimulates the cochlear nuclear complex in the brainstem directly.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: True about BAHA: [AIIMS May 13]

options.text: Useful in canal atresia and microtia
Useful after surgery in neurofibromatosis 2 for acoustic neuroma

questions.answerText: Useful in canal atresia and microtia
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 122, 123.
BAHA: Bone anchored hearing aid is a type of hearing aid which is based on the principle of bone conduction. BAHA uses a surgically implanted abutment to transmit sound by direct conduction through bone to cochlea, bypassing the external auditory canal and middle ear.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: Father of neuro-otology is: [AIIMS May 2013]

Ref: Internet search.
Note: For severe bilateral SNHL - Cochlear implant is used. For bilateral acoustic neuromas in Neurofibromatosis - auditory brainstem implant is used.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: All are true about cochlear implant except: [AIIMS 2009]

options.text: Switch on is done after 3 weeks
MRI has no role in preop assessment

questions.answerText: MRI has no role in preop assessment
questions.explanation:
Lets see each option separately:
Option a: Minimum age 1 year - correct
Option b: PTA of 70 dB or more - correct as cochlear implant is useful in B/L severe hearing loss >70 dB.
Option c: Switch on is done after 3 weeks - correct. Remember after placing an implant, a gap of 2-3 weeks is given for the wound to heal before the implant is to activated. Activation does not produce instant hearing.
Option d: MRI has no role is preop assessment - incorrect. Preop investigation done before an implant is placed: Complete audiological evaluation, HRCT, MRI.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: A two year old child was planned for brain stem implant. All are indications of brain stem implant except: [AIIMS 2004]
questions.explanation:
Ref: Dhingra 6/e, p 115.
In Mondini deformity the defect is at the level of cochlea, which can be corrected by cochlear implant.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: Which of the following part of cochlear implant is implanted during surgery: [AIIMS May 2014]
questions.explanation:
Ref: Dhingra 6/e, p 124. A cochlear implant has an external and internal component.
Components of cochlear implants
External component (remain outside the body)
Internal component (fitted inside the body)
• Microphone
• Receiver/stimulator (implanted under the skin)
• Speech-processor
• Electrode array (implanted in the scala tympani of the cochlea)
• Transmitter

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 13: Rehabilitative Methods
questions.stem: What is placed during surgery for cochlear implant: [AIIMS Nov 2013]
questions.explanation:
Ref: Dhingra 4/e, p 121-123; Dhingra 6/e, p 124.
Receiver/Stimulator (Implanted under the skin) and Electrode array (Implanted in the scala tympani of the cochlea) are the part of internal component of cochlear implant, which are fitted inside the body.
Microphone, Speech-processor and Transmitter are the part of external component of cochlear implant, which remain outside the body.
END OF CHAPTER 13 MCQs
This completes Chapter 13 (Rehabilitative Methods) with all MCQs, explanations, and relevant theory content integrated. The chapter now covers:
Hearing Aids - Components (Microphone, Amplifier, Receiver), Types (Conventional, Programmable analogue, Digital), Styles (CIC, ITC, ITE, BTE), Indications, Disadvantages
Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) - Indications (Canal atresia, Congenital malformation, Chronic ear discharge, Conductive/mixed hearing loss where surgery contraindicated, Single-sided hearing loss)
Vibrant Sound Bridge/Implantable Hearing Aid - Direct stimulation of ossicles, Candidate profile (Adult >18 years, Moderate-to-severe SNHL), Advantages (Better sound quality, Less wax problems, Less feedback)
Cochlear Implants - Electronic device, Bypasses cochlea, Replaces organ of corti, Indications (B/L severe hearing loss >70 dB, Not benefitted by hearing aids, Auditory neuropathy, Mondini aplasia), Components (External: Microphone, Speech processor, Transmitter; Internal: Receiver/stimulator, Electrode array in scala tympani), Prerequisites (Intact VIII nerve, At least 1 year of age, Postlingual > Prelingual, SDS < 50%), Surgical approach (Facial recess approach/Posterior tympanotomy, Veria technique), Contraindications (Absence of cochlea, Absent cochlear nerve), Invented by Dr William F. House, Activation after 3-4 weeks, Mapping
Auditory Brainstem Implants (ABI) - Stimulates cochlear nuclear complex, Lateral recess of fourth ventricle, Indicated when CN VIII severed (B/L acoustic neuroma/NF-2), Auditory midbrain implant (Inferior colliculus)
okay

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 14: Miscellaneous · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Laser uvulopharyngopalatoplasty is the surgery done for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Ref: Mohan Bansal Textbook of Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat 1/e, p 435.
Snoring: Noisy breathing, a rough, rattling inspiratory noise produced by vibration of pendulous soft palate or occasionally of vocal cords, during sleep.
Snoring indicates some obstruction in upper airway and represents a continuum of the similar pathology as of Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), where snoring is on one end and OSA on the other.
Management of snoring without Obstructive Sleep Apnea:Uvulopalatoplasty - Laser Assisted Uvulopalatoplasty (LAUP) or Bovie-Assisted Uvulopalatoplasty (BAUP). It can be performed under Local Anaesthesia in OPD. In this procedure uvula is amputated and 1 cm trenches are created in the soft palate on either side of uvula. The soft palate elevates and stiffens after healing.
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty - It is the M/C surgery performed for Obstructive Sleep Apnea. It is also very effective in treating snoring.
Also Know:OSA - Obstructive sleep apnea is a disorder characterised by loud, habitual snoring and repetitive obstruction of the upper airway during sleep, resulting in prolonged intervals of hypoxia and fragmented sleep.
Gold standard test in evaluation of OSA - Polysomnography. It differentiates snoring without OSA from snoring with OSA and also identifies the severity of apnea.
Muller's maneuver - This test is done before uvulopalatopharyngoplasty to know whether the patient will benefit from the surgery or not.

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra - read below.
Condition
Points in favour

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 14: Miscellaneous · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Gustatory sweating and flushing (Frey's syndrome) follows damage to the: [JIPMER 80; DNB 91]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Maqbool 11/e, p 276; S. Das Short Cases of Clinical Surgery 3/e, p 82.
Auriculotemporal syndrome (Syn. Frey's Syndrome): Partial injury to the auriculotemporal nerve gives rise to such syndrome. This type of injury:
May be congenital, possibly due to birth trauma.
May be accidental injury.
May be caused by inadvertent incision for drainage of parotid abscess.
May occasionally follow superficial parotidectomy.
Clinical features: There is flushing and sweating of the skin innervated by the auriculotemporal nerve particularly during meal and presence of cutaneous hyperaesthesia in front and above the ear (the area supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve).
The Explanation of this syndrome is:
The postganglionic parasympathetic fibres become united to the sympathetic nerves from the superior cervical ganglion which are concerned to supply vessels and sweat glands of that region. This causes flushing and sweating of the skin.
Following injury to the auriculotemporal nerve, postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the otic ganglion grow down the sheaths of the cutaneous filaments, so hyperaesthesia follows stimulation of the secretomotor nerves.
Treatment: If the symptoms persist, the treatment is avulsion of the auriculotemporal nerve in front of the auricle where it lies just posterior to the superficial temporal vessels.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 14: Miscellaneous · New-pattern question
questions.stem: A patient has bilateral conductive deafness, tinnitus with positive family history. The diagnosis: [AIIMS 93]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 30, 87.
Conductive deafness means the disease process leading to deafness is limited to external ear, tympanic membrane, middle ear including the footplate of stapes.
Bilateral conductive deafness rules out Meniere's disease (as it presents with SNHL).
Amongst the remaining three options, positive family history is seen mainly in case of otosclerosis (Otospongiosis), so it is our answer.

questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 41; Scott-Brown's Otolaryngology 7/e, vol 3, Chap 238 p 3539. It is mid to late adult onset, bilateral, progressive sensorineural hearing loss, where underlying causes have been excluded.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 14: Miscellaneous · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Second primary tumor of head and neck is most commonly seen in malignancy of: [AIIMS May 2012]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Internet search.
Patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) are at increased risk for the development of second primary malignancies compared with the general population. These second primary malignancies typically develop in the aerodigestive tract (lung, head and neck, esophagus). The most frequent second primary malignancy is lung cancer. The highest relative increase in risk is for a second head and neck cancer. The site of the index cancer influences the most likely site of a second primary malignancy. In patients with an index malignancy of the larynx, the second primary tumor was commonly seen in lung, while in patients with an index malignancy of the oral cavity, the second primary tumor was commonly seen in head and neck or esophagus.
The criteria for classifying a tumor as a second primary malignancy are:
Histologic confirmation of malignancy in both the index and secondary tumors.
There should be at least 2 cm of normal mucosa between the tumors.
If the tumors are in the same location, then they should be separated in time by at least five years.
Metastatic tumor should be excluded.
