questions.explanation:
Ref. Hazarika ENT 3/e, p 231.
Columella: It is the part between the two anterior nostrils or the part between the two nasal vestibules. It forms the caudal part of nasal septum. It is formed by medial crura of the two lower lateral cartilages.
Root of nose: The upper angle of the nose where it is continuous with forehead is called as root of the nose. The deepest point at the root of nose where the two nasal bones meet the frontal bone is called as nasion, i.e. here two bones meet.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Osseocartilaginous junction on the dorsum of nose is:
questions.explanation: Rhinion: The point where the lower end of internasal suture, i.e. suture between two nasal bones meets with the lower cartilaginous part of the nose, i.e. here bone is meeting cartilage. So rhinion is osseocartilaginous junction.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Nasal valve is bounded by all except:
questions.explanation: Internal nasal valve: It is bounded laterally by limen nasi and inferior turbinate, medially by nasal septum (cartilaginous part) and inferiorly by the floor of pyriform aperture.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Internal nasal valve is bounded by:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra ENT 6/e, p 135.
Internal nasal valve: It is bounded laterally by limen nasi (lower edge of upper lateral cartilage) and inferior turbinate, medially by nasal septum (cartilaginous part) and inferiorly by the floor of pyriform aperture.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Patency of nasal valve is checked by:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Mohan Bansal Essentials of ENT 1/e, p 188.
Cottle test is done for checking the patency of nasal valve. The cheek is drawn laterally and patient breathes quietly. If there is subjective improvement in nasal airway, the test is considered positive and indicates nasal valve compromise.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Which of the following is an independent bone:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra ENT 6/e, p 135. Inferior turbinate is a separate bone, rest all are a part of ethmoidal labyrinth.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Supreme turbinate is another name for:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra ENT 6/e, p 138. Supreme turbinate is the fourth turbinate which is sometimes present. It is seen above superior turbinate.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Sphenopalatine foramen is related to:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Hazarika ENT 3/e, p 233. The posterior end of middle turbinate points to the opening of sphenopalatine foramen.
Also know: Sphenopalatine foramen is a route of communication between nasal cavity and pterygopalatine fossa. Major structures passing through the foramen are:
Sphenopalatine branch of maxillary artery
Nasopalatine branch of maxillary nerve
Superior nasal branch of maxillary nerve.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: All of the following drain in middle meatus except:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra ENT 6/e, p 135. Nasolacrimal duct opens in inferior meatus, rest all structures open in middle meatus.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Anterior ethmoidal artery arises from:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 176. Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries are branches of ophthalmic artery which is a branch of internal carotid artery.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Which of the following is not a function of nose:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 141. Read the text for explanation.
The functions of nose are:
Olfaction
Respiration
Air conditioning of respired air (humidification and temperature control)
Protection of lower airway
Vocal resonance
Nasal reflex

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Ciliary movement rate of nasal mucosa is:
questions.explanation: The cilia of nasal mucosa beat constantly at speed of 5-10 mm/minutes.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Parosmia is:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 157; 6/e, p 142.
Disorders of smell:
Anosmia: Total loss of sense of smell
Hyposmia: Partial loss of sense of smell
Parosmia: Perversion of smell (seen in recovery phase of post influenzal anosmia; intracranial tumors).

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Nasal cycle is the cyclical alternate nasal blockage occurring:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 140; Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 40.
Nasal cycle: The alternate opening and closing of each side of nose is called nasal cycle.
Kayser first described nasal cycle in 1895
There is rhythmic cyclical congestion and decongestion of nasal mucosa
Nasal cycle varies every 2½-4 hrs and is characteristic of an individual.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Function of mucociliary action of upper respiratory tract is:

options.text: Increased the velocity of inspired air
Traps the pathogenic organisms in inspired air

questions.answerText: Traps the pathogenic organisms in inspired air
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 141-142. Nasal mucosa contains goblet cells for secretion of mucus, which forms a mucus blanket. The inspired bacteria, viruses and dust particles are entrapped on this viscous mucus blanket. Hence mucociliary action is protective.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Movement of mucous in nose is by:
questions.explanation: As discussed in previous Question - movement of mucus in nose is mainly by mucociliary action.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Odour receptors are present in:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 142. Odor receptors are present in olfactory epithelium lining the olfactory region of nose.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Thudichum speculum is used for visualizing:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Tuli 1/e, p 538; 2/e, p 503; Mohan Bansal p 281. Thudichum speculum or Vienna type speculum is used to visualize anterior nasal cavity (examination is called anterior rhinoscopy).
NOTE: Posterior nares can be visualized during posterior rhinoscopy using posterior nasal mirror.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Which is not visualized on posterior rhinoscopy:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Maqbool 11/e, p 164.
Posterior rhinoscopy: It is method of examination of the posterior aspect of nose and pharynx. Structures seen during rhinoscopy are:
Both choanae
Posterior end of nasal septum
Opening of Eustachian tube
Posterior end of superior/middle and inferior turbinates
Fossa of Rosenmuller
Torus Tubarius
Adenoids
Roof and posterior wall and nasopharynx.
Inferior meatus is not visualized on posterior rhinoscopy.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Frontonasal duct opens into: [PGI 98]
questions.explanation: Ref. Turner 10/e, p 379; Dhingra 5/e, p 178; 6/e, p 136, 137; TB of Mohan Bansal p 34, 35, 37.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Frontal sinus drain into: [PGI 97, 98]
questions.explanation: Frontal sinus drains into middle meatus via frontonasal duct.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Paranasal sinus opening in middle meatus: [PGI 03, 98]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 152, 153; Tuli 1/e, p 135-136; Logan Turner 10/e, p 379; TB of Mohan Bansal p 34.
Middle meatus lies between the middle and inferior turbinates and is important because of the presence of osteomeatal complex in this area.
Part of lateral nasal wall
Openings
Inferior meatus
Nasolacrimal duct
Middle meatus
Frontal sinus (which opens via frontonasal duct), Maxillary sinus, Anterior ethmoidal sinus
Superior meatus
Posterior ethmoidal sinus
Sphenoethmoidal recess
Sphenoid sinus

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: The maxillary sinus opens into middle meatus at the level of: [DNB 02]
questions.explanation: The natural ostium of the maxillary sinus opens into the hiatus semilunaris and is located between the anteroinferior part of the bulla and the uncinate process.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: All drains into middle meatus except: [DNB 02]
questions.explanation: Nasolacrimal duct opens into inferior meatus.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Hiatus semilunaris is present in: [CUPGEE 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 152, 153; Tuli 1/e, p 135-136.
Hiatus semilunaris is a slitlike semilunar shaped opening present below the bulla ethmoidalis in the middle meatus.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Bulla ethmoidalis is seen in: [AIIMS 92]
questions.explanation: Bulla ethmoidalis is a rounded prominence seen posterosuperior to the uncinate process in the middle meatus. It represents the middle ethmoidal air cells.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Opening of posterior ethmoid sinus is in: [Jharkhand 06]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, 153, 6/e, p 138. Posterior ethmoidal sinus opens into superior meatus (which lies lateral to superior turbinate).

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Sphenoidal sinus opens into: [Kerala 98]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 153; 6/e, p 138; TB of Mohan Bansal p 38. Sphenoethmoid recess is situated above the superior turbinate and receives opening of sphenoidal sinus.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Nasolacrimal duct opens into: [MAHE 05]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 150; 6/e, p 135.
Nasolacrimal duct opens into inferior meatus below the level of inferior turbinate
Nasolacrimal duct is guarded at its terminal end by a mucosal valve k/a Hasner's valve
Frontonasal duct opens into middle meatus.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Inferior turbinate is a: [JIPMER 04]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 150; 6/e, p 135; Tuli 1/e, p 135; 2/e, p 140. The inferior turbinate is a separate bone, while rest of the turbinates are a part of ethmoidal labyrinth.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Ethmoid bone forms A/E: [Bihar 05]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 12; Tuli 1/e, p 135; 2/e, p 140. "The inferior turbinate is a separate bone, while rest of the turbinates are a part of ethmoidal labyrinth."

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Which of the following is known as fourth turbinate: [UP 01]
questions.explanation: Supreme turbinate is the fourth turbinate which is sometimes present above the superior turbinate.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Turbinate that articulates with ethmoid is: [AP 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scotts Brown 7/e, Vol 2 p 1329; Dhingra 6/e, p 136.
Middle turbinate and superior turbinate are a part of the ethmoidal bone whereas inferior turbinate is an independent bone which articulates with the ethmoid bone, completing the medial wall of nasolacrimal duct.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: External nose is formed from: [AP 96]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 149, 150; 6/e, p 134; TB of Mohan Bansal p 30.
External nose is made up of bony framework which forms upper third part and cartilaginous forms lower two-third part framework.
Cartilages of nose:
Paired upper lateral nasal cartilages
Paired lower nasal cartilages
Lesser alar (sesamoid) cartilages - 2 or more in number
Unpaired septal cartilage.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Choana is: [TN 03]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Turner 10/e, p 4; Dhingra 5/e, p 150; 6/e, p 135.
Nasal cavity: "Nasal fossae are two irregular cavities extending from the mucocutaneous junction with the nasal vestibule in front (the anterior nares) to the junction with the nasopharynx behind (posterior nares or choanae)."
"Each nasal cavity communicates with the external through naris or nares and with nasopharynx through posterior nasal aperture or choana." Ref. Dhingra 6/e, 135.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Direction of nasolacrimal duct is: [AI 99]
questions.explanation:
Ref. TB of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 42.
Nasolacrimal duct: It is a membranous passage which begins at the lower end of the lacrimal sac. It runs downward, backward and laterally and opens in the inferior meatus of the nose. A fold of mucous membrane called the valve of Hasner forms an imperfect valve at the lower end of the duct.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Which of the following bones do not contribute the nasal septum: [AI 03]
questions.explanation:
Ref. BDC 4/e, Vol 3 p 228-229; Dhingra 5/e, p 162; 6/e, p 147.
Nasal septum is the osseocartilagenous partition between the two halves of nasal cavity.
Its constituents are:(i) Osseous part:
The vomer
Perpendicular plate of ethmoid
Nasal crest of nasal bone
Nasal spine of frontal bone
Nasal crest of palatine bone
Nasal crest of maxillary bone
Rostrum of sphenoid bone
(ii) Cartilaginous part: Septal (Quadrilateral) cartilage
Lacrimal bone does not contribute to the nasal septum.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Quadrilateral cartilage is attached to all except: [DNB 01]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1326; Dhingra 6/e, p 147.
Quadrilateral cartilage or septal cartilage forms the nasal septum. The anterior side of this cartilage forms the dorsum of external nose. It comes in contact with perpendicular plate of ethmoid, vomer and anterior nasal spine. It does not attach to sphenoid.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: All these structures are found in the lateral nasal wall except: [MP 07]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2 p 1329-1330; Dhingra 5/e, p 150-153; 6/e, p 134-138.
The lateral nasal wall is composed of three turbinates:
Superior turbinate
Middle turbinate
Inferior turbinate
Below each turbinate is the respective meatus:
Inferior meatus
Middle meatus
Superior meatus
Above the superior turbinate lies the sphenoethmoid recess.
Just anterior to the middle meatus, is a small crest/mound on the lateral wall called as Agger nasi.
In the inferior meatus - opens the nasolacrimal duct guarded at its terminal end by a mucosal valve k/a Hasner's valve.
NOTE: Vomer is an independent bone which forms the posteroinferior part of nasal septum (i.e. medial wall of nose).

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Nasal valve is formed by all except: [MP 08]

options.text: Lower end of upper lateral cartilage

questions.explanation:
Ref. Scotts Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1358; Dhingra 5/e, p 150; 6/e, p 138; TB of Mohan Bansal p 287.
Anterior Nasal Valve/Internal Nasal Valve:
This is the narrowest part of nose and is less well defined physiologically than anatomically.
It is formed by the lower edge of the upper lateral cartilages (limen nasi), the anterior end of the inferior turbinate and the adjacent septum.
Middle turbinate does not form part of the nasal valve.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Onodi cells and Haller cells are seen in relation to: [AIIMS Nov 09]

options.text: Optic nerve and floor of orbit
Optic nerve and ethmoidal air cells

questions.answerText: Optic nerve and floor of orbit
questions.explanation:
Ref. Grays 40/e, p 558; Dhingra 5/e, p 153; 6/e, p 136; TB of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 38.
Onodi cells: They are the most posterior ethmoidal air cells. They are surgically important as they are related to optic nerve and internal carotid artery.
Haller cells: These are ethmoidal cells in floor of orbit.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Osteomeatal complex (OMC) connects: [MH 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2 p 1345.
Osteomeatal complex lies in the middle meatus. It is the final common drainage pathway for the maxillary, frontal and anterior ethmoid sinuses into the nasal cavity (so will obviously connect any of these to the nasal cavity).

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Nasal mucosa is supplied by: [AI 92]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 189, 190.
Both internal carotid artery and external carotid artery supply the nose but main artery is the external carotid artery.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: During inspiration the main current of airflow in a normal nasal cavity is through: [AI 07]

options.text: Middle part of the cavity in middle meatus in a parabolic curve
Lower part of the cavity in the inferior meatus in a parabolic curve
Superior part of the cavity in the superior meatus

questions.answerText: Middle part of the cavity in middle meatus in a parabolic curve
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 155; 6/e, p 140.
Nose is the natural pathway for breathing.
During quiet respiration:
Inspiratory air current passes through middle part of nose between the turbinates and nasal septum.
Very little air passes through inferior meatus or olfactory region of nose. Therefore, weak odorous substances have to be sniffed before they can reach olfactory area.
During expiration, air current follows the same course as during inspiration, but the entire air current is not expelled directly through the nares.
Friction offered at limen nasi converts it into eddies under cover of inferior and middle turbinates and thus sinuses are ventilated during expiration.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Function of mucociliary action of upper respiratory tract is: [Kerala 94]

options.text: Increase the velocity of inspired air
Traps the pathogenic organisms in inspired air

questions.answerText: Traps the pathogenic organisms in inspired air
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 156; 6/e, p 140. The inspired bacteria, viruses and dust particles are entrapped on this viscous mucus blanket. Hence mucociliary action is protective.

questions.chapter: Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 15: Anatomy and Physiology of Nose
questions.stem: Veins not involved in spreading infection to cavernous sinus from danger area of face:
questions.explanation:
Ref. BD Chaurasia p 62, 63; Maqbool 11/e, p 172.
Dangerous area of face includes upper lip and anteroinferior part of nose including the vestibule. This area freely communicates with the cavernous sinus through a set of valveless veins, anterior facial vein and superior ophthalmic vein. Any infection of this area can thus travel intracranially leading to meningitis and cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Veins draining dangerous area - Maqbool 11/e, p 172:
Through facial veins communicating with ophthalmic veins (both having no valve)
Through the pterygoid plexus of veins which communicate with facial vein on one hand and the cavernous sinus through emissary vein on the other hand.
According to B.D. Chaurasia Vol 3, 5/e, p 62:Deep connections of the facial vein include:
A communication between the supraorbital and superior ophthalmic veins.
Another with the pterygoid plexus through the deep facial vein which passes backwards over the buccinator.
The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus through these connections. Infections from the face can spread in a retrograde direction and cause thrombosis of the cavernous sinus. This is specially likely to occur in the presence of infection in the upper lip and in the lower part of the nose. This area is, therefore, called the dangerous area of the face.
Lingual vein and cephalic vein are not involved in spreading infection to cavernous sinus from dangerous area of face.
END OF CHAPTER 15 MCQs
This completes Chapter 15 (Anatomy and Physiology of Nose) with all MCQs, explanations, and relevant theory content integrated. The chapter now covers:
External Nose - Pyramidal structure, Bony part (Paired nasal bone, Frontal process of maxilla, Nasal process of frontal bone), Cartilaginous part (3 paired + 1 unpaired cartilages), Rhinion, Nasion, Columella, Limen nasi
Internal Nose - Nasal vestibule (Stratified squamous epithelium, Hair follicles, Vibrissae, Sebaceous glands, Sweat glands), Nasal cavity proper
Internal Nasal Valve - Bounded by limen nasi, inferior turbinate, nasal septum, floor of pyriform aperture, Cottle test
Lateral Nasal Wall - Turbinates (Superior, Middle, Inferior - separate bone, Supreme - fourth turbinate), Meatuses (Inferior, Middle, Superior), Sphenoethmoidal recess
Middle Meatus - Openings (Maxillary, Frontal, Anterior ethmoids), Osteomeatal complex (Uncinate process, Bulla ethmoidalis, Hiatus semilunaris, Ethmoidal infundibulum, Frontal recess)
Inferior Meatus - Nasolacrimal duct opening (Hasner's valve)
Superior Meatus - Posterior ethmoidal sinus opening
Sphenoethmoidal Recess - Sphenoid sinus opening
Ethmoidal Air Cells - Anterior (Bulla ethmoidalis, Agger nasi, Haller cells), Middle, Posterior (Onodi cells)
Nasal Septum - Columellar, Membranous, Septum proper (Septal cartilage, Perpendicular plate of ethmoid, Vomer), Other contributors
Blood Supply - Internal carotid (Ophthalmic → Anterior and Posterior ethmoidal), External carotid (Facial → Superior labial; Maxillary → Greater palatine, Sphenopalatine → Artery of epistaxis), Little's area, Kiesselbach plexus
Nerve Supply - Vidian nerve (Nerve of pterygoid canal), Nasopalatine, Anterior ethmoidal, Anterior superior alveolar
Lymphatic Drainage - Submandibular nodes, Upper jugular nodes, Retropharyngeal nodes
Dangerous Area of Face - Upper lip, Anteroinferior part of nose, Vestibule, Communicates with cavernous sinus through valveless veins (Facial vein, Superior ophthalmic vein, Pterygoid plexus)
Ethmoid Bone - Laterally (Turbinates, Lamina papyracea, Uncinate process), Medially (Perpendicular plate), Superiorly (Cribriform plate)
Gateways - Cribriform plate (Olfactory nerve), Sphenopalatine foramen (Sphenopalatine branch of maxillary artery, Nasopalatine nerve, Superior nasal nerve), Incisive canal (Nasopalatine nerve, Greater palatine artery)
Physiology - Olfaction, Respiration, Air conditioning, Protection, Vocal resonance, Nasal reflex, Nasal cycle (Kayser, 2½-4 hrs), Mucociliary clearance (5-10 mm/min), Kartagener's syndrome (Immotile cilia, Bronchiectasis, Situs inversus)
Examination - Anterior rhinoscopy (Thudichum speculum), Posterior rhinoscopy (Postnasal mirror)
continue

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Crooked nose is due to:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 143; Essentials of ENT, Mohan Bansal, 1/e, p 197.
In crooked nose, the midline of dorsum (obviously along with septa) from frontonasal angle to the tip of nose is curved in a C- or S-shaped manner.

questions.stem: All are true about Rhinophyma except:

options.text: Also called as elephantiasis of nose
Most commonly due to diabetes mellitus

questions.answerText: Most commonly due to diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation:
Ref. TB of ENT, Hazarika 3/e, p 268; Dhingra 6/e, p 144.
Remember: Sebaceous glands are a variety of holocrine glands. Rest all discussed in text.
Rhinophyma is a slow-growing benign tumor which occurs due to hypertrophy of the sebaceous glands of the tip of the nose. Seen in long standing cases of acne rosacea. Mostly affects men past middle age. Presents as a pink, lobulated mass over the nose.

questions.stem: Rhinophyma is associated with:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 144. See the text for explanation.
Rhinophyma is a slow-growing benign tumor which occurs due to hypertrophy of the sebaceous glands of the tip of the nose.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum · New-pattern question
questions.stem: A polypoidal swelling is noted in an infant near the glabella. The swelling is compressible and increases in size on coughing. All of the following investigations should be done except:
questions.explanation:
Ref. TB of ENT, Hazarika, 3/e p 263.
In the question, as infant is presenting with a polypoidal compressible mass near the glabella, it should raise the suspicion of a frontal encephalocele. In all such cases, remember never do a Biopsy: as it can lead to CSF Rhinorrhea.
NOTE: An encephalocele can present as pulsatile swelling in the midline at the root of nose glabella (Nasofrontal variety), side of nose (Nasoethmoidal variety) or on the anterior middle aspect of the orbit (naso-orbital variety).

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Frustenberg sign is positive in:
questions.explanation:
Ref. TB of ENT, Hazarika 3/e, p 263.
Furstenberg test: Bilateral compression of internal jugular vein leading to increase in size of mass is positive Furstenberg test, seen in case of nasal encephalocele.
In nasal gliomas and dermoid cyst—Furstenberg test is negative.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum · New-pattern question
questions.stem: A 2 years old infant is bought to OPD by the mother with case of frequent nasal blockage. On examination a solitary polypoidal mass is seen to arise from the roof of the nose. First step in investigation is:
questions.explanation:
A solitary polypoidal mass arising from roof of the nose in an infant should raise the suspicion of encephalocele.
Remember: M/C age of presentation of encephalocele is 15-24 months of age. In such cases biopsy should never be attempted as discussed it can result in CSF rhinorrhea. First investigation done is CT scan. IOC is MRI.

questions.stem: What is not true about septal hematoma:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Essentials of ENT, Mohan Bansal, p 231, 232.
Septal hematoma should not be left to resolve spontaneously as the blood supply of septal cartilage is deprived in this case. Thus surgical management as outlined in the text should be performed as early as possible.

questions.stem: Nasal septum abscess leads to:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Essentials of ENT, Mohan Bansal, p 232.
Complications of Septal Abscess:
Saddle nose deformity: The necrosis of septal cartilage causes depression of the nasal dorsum in the supratip area. It needs augmentation rhinoplasty, which is performed after 2-3 months.
Septal perforation due to necrosis of septal flaps.
Meningitis.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: True about rhinophyma: [AI 01]

options.text: Treatment is shaving, dermabrasion and skin grafting.

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 144; TB of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 292.
Rhinophyma is a slow-growing benign tumor which occurs due to hypertrophy of the sebaceous glands of the tip of the nose.
Seen in long standing cases of acne rosacea.
Mostly affects men past middle age.
Presents as a pink, lobulated mass over the nose.
Treatment:
Paring down the bulk of the tumor with a sharp knife, or carbon dioxide laser or scalpel (dermabrasion), and the area is allowed to re-epithelize.
Sometimes tumor is completely excised and the raw area is covered with skin graft.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Most common presentation of infant with bilateral choanal atresia: [AIIMS 96]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Turner 10/e, p 379; Dhingra 6/e, p 163; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 337.
Choanal atresia is usually U/L.
If it occurs bilaterally the neonate presents with difficulty in breathing as infant is a nose breather and does not breathe from mouth. The neonate may have asphyxia and bilateral blockage of nose that also makes suckling difficult.
U/L atresia presents with nasal obstruction including snoring but goes unidentified till adult life.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Choanal atresia is associated with: [PGI 08]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1 p 1071; Dhingra 6/e, p 163; OP Ghai 6 and 7/e, p 336, 337.
Choanal atresia is associated with CHARGE syndrome: Coloboma of eye, Heart defects, Atresia of choana, Retarded growth, Genital defects and Ear defects.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Which of the following procedure is helpful in diagnosis of choanal atresia: [PGI May 2012]
questions.explanation:
"Structures normally seen on posterior rhinoscopy are choanal polyp or atresia" - Dhingra 5/e, p 385.
"Choanal atresia: Posterior rhinoscopy may be undertaken in older children and will show the occlusion." - Turner 10/e, p 380.
Thus posterior rhinoscopy and not anterior rhinoscopy are useful in the diagnosis of choanal atresia.
"Acoustic rhinometry is a new technique which evaluates nasal obstruction by analysing reflections of a sound pulse introduced via the nostrils. The technique is rapid, reproducible, non-invasive and requires minimal cooperation from the subject. A graph of nasal cross-sectional area as a function of distance from the nostril is produced, from which several area and volume estimates of the nasal cavity can be derived. The role of acoustic rhinometry in diagnosis is somewhat limited compared to nasal endoscopy, but it is useful for nasal challenge and for quantifying nasal obstruction. It is helpful in evaluating childhood nasal obstruction, as it is well tolerated by children as young as 3 years old - a group of patients to whom objective tests have hitherto been difficult to apply."

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: All are true about nasolabial cysts except: [AIIMS Nov 08]
questions.explanation:
Ref. http://www.maxillofacialcentre.com./Bondbook/softissue/nasolabialcyst.html#introduction; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2 p 1320; Textbook of ENT, Hazarika, p 367.
Nasolabial Cysts/Nasoalveolar Cyst/Klestadt's Cyst
It is a rare non-odontogenic cyst which occurs in the region of nasolabial fold. It may arise from epithelial entrapment in the line of fusion between medial and lateral nasal process during the development of nose and cheek (hence also called epithelial inclusion cyst) or may arise as epithelial remnants of nasolacrimal duct.
Female > Male
Bilateral in approximately 10% of all cases.
Usually present in 4th and 5th decades of life.
It presents as a smooth and soft bulge in the region of nasolabial fold.
Large cyst obliterates the nasolabial sulcus.
Treatment is by surgical excision using sublabial approach.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Depressed bridge of the nose may be due to any of the following except: [DNB 03]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 143.
Depressed nasal bridge results from sagging of the bridge of nose either due to injury or infection of osseous or cartilaginous part of the bridge of nose.
Causes of depressed nose/saddle nose are (Mnemonic – HOT SALT):
H = Hematoma
O = Operative, i.e. excessive removal of septum during submucous resection
T = Trauma
S = Syphilis
A = Abscess
L = Leprosy
T = Tuberculosis
Thalassemia can cause depressed nasal bridge due to marrow hyperplasia. Acromegaly does not cause depressed nasal bridge.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: A crooked nose is due to: [PAL 2000]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 143; Textbook of Mohan Bansal, p 291.
In crooked nose, the dorsum of nose is deviated but tip is in midline.
In a deviated nose, both dorsum and tip are deviated.
Saddle nose is depressed nasal dorsum which may involve only cartilaginous or both bony and cartilaginous components.
Humped nose, there is a presence of hump on nose.
NOTE: Both crooked nose and saddle nose are managed by septo-rhinoplasty whereas humped nose is managed by reduction rhinoplasty.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Percentage of newborns with deviation of nasal septum: [PGI 93]
questions.explanation: Ref. Turner 10/e, p 21. Around 60% of children are born with some degree of nasal deviation.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Features associated with DNS include all of the following except: [AI 98]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 149; Tuli 1/e, p 153; Textbook of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 334, 335.
In deviated nasal septum, the nasal chamber on the concave side of the nasal septum is wide and shows compensatory hypertrophy of turbinates and not atrophy.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: DNS may be associated with all the following except: [PGI]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 149; Tuli 1/e, p 153; Textbook of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 334, 335.
In deviated nasal septum, the nasal chamber on the concave side of the nasal septum is wide and shows compensatory hypertrophy of turbinates and not atrophy.
The sphenoid sinus opens in the sphenoethmoid recess near the roof of nasal cavity and this opening is not affected by DNS.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: For deviated nasal septum, surgery is required for: [PGI 01]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 413, 415; Tuli 1/e, p 507; 2/e, p 516.
Indications for Surgery in DNS
Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent headaches
Deviation causing recurrent sinusitis or otitis media
Recurrent epistaxis from septal spur
Access for operation in polypectomy with DNS
As a part of septorhinoplasty for cosmetic correction of external nasal deformities.
As an approach to hypophysectomy
NOTE: If instead of marked septal deviation, the option could have been only 'septal deviation' then remember minor degree of septal deviation not causing any symptoms does not require any treatment.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: All of the following true of septoplasty operation for DNS except: [UPSC]

options.text: Preferably done after 16 years of age
Done in some cases of epistaxis

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 413.
In septoplasty, the mucoperichondrium is preserved (not removed). Only the most deviated parts are removed. Rest of the septal framework is corrected and reposited by plastic means.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Alternative for SMR: [DNB 01]
questions.explanation: Septoplasty is the conservative alternative to Submucous Resection (SMR). It is the preferred operation these days.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Killian's incision is used for: [TN 04]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 413.
Killian's incision is given at 1.25 cm behind the columella at the mucocutaneous junction at the convex side of the deviation for submucous resection of nasal septum.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Which is not done in septoplasty: [St. Johns 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Lees Synopsis of Anaesthesia 13/e, pp 734, 735.
"Intranasal operations are polypectomy, septoplasty, rhinoplasty and functional endoscopic sinus surgery. Either a laryngeal mask or a cuffed endotracheal tube may be used with a throat pack, depending on the anesthetist's confidence, the surgeon, the amount of blood loss and the duration of surgery. A flexible laryngeal mask or south-facing preformed tube allows the airway to be secured away from the nose."
"Topical nasal vasoconstriction is extremely useful and may be applied by the anesthetist or surgeon. Commonly used vasoconstrictors include 5-10% cocaine, cocaine paste, xylometazoline or ephedrine drops or spray, Moffett's solution, or dental cartridge injection of local anesthetic with epinephrine (adrenaline) 1:80,000."
"Surgery is easier with controlled hypotension. Profuse bleeding may cause the operation to be abandoned."
Intraoperative and Postoperative Considerations
"The most important consideration of nasal surgery is achieving profound vasoconstriction in the nares to minimize and control bleeding. This vasoconstriction can be achieved with cocaine packs, local anesthetics, and epinephrine infiltration."
"A moderate degree of controlled hypotension combined with head elevation decreases bleeding in the surgical site."
"Placing an oropharyngeal pack or suctioning the stomach at the conclusion of surgery may attenuate postoperative retching and vomiting."
Thus in any nasal surgery:
Elective hypotension
Throat pack all can be done
Nasal preparation with 10% cocaine

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Which of the following surgery is not contraindicated below 12 years of age? [MH 03]
questions.explanation: Amongst all options, FESS is the only surgery which can be performed before 17 years. Remember ideally none of the forms of septal surgery can be performed before 17 years. Still in rarest circumstances, septal surgery has to performed in children septoplasty is done and never SMR.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: To prevent synechiae formation after nasal surgery, which one of the following packings is the most useful: [AIIMS Nov 04]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Journal of Laryngology and Otology 06, Vol 120, p 921-923 ISSN 00222151.
After Nasal surgery it has been seen that mitomycin drops applied over nasal mucosa decrease nasal synechiae formation. This is the newer approach and several trials are being done on it... but our standard textbooks have not yet included it.
"The nasal cavities are packed with ribbon gauze impregnated with Vaseline or liquid paraffin to prevent its sticking to nasal mucosa." - Scott Brown 7/e, p 1602.
"Ribbon gauze impregnated with petroleum jelly or bismuth iodoform paraffin paste (BIPP) is inserted in the entire length of the nasal cavity in an attempt to tamponade the bleeding." - Scott Brown 7/e, p 1602.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: True about septal hematoma is: [PGI 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 150; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 336.
Septal hematoma occurs due to trauma, can lead to saddle nose deformity (if infected leading to septal abscess and cartilage necrosis), and may lead to abscess formation. Treatment is surgical (aspiration or incision and drainage), not conservative.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Bony septal perforation occurs in: [Karnataka 95]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 151; Scott Brown Otolaryngology 7/e, Vol 2, Chapter 124, p 1583.
Cause of Perforation of:
Bony septum
Cartilaginous septum
Whole septum
Syphilis
Lupus, Leprosy, Tuberculosis
Wegener's granuloma (which includes bony septum also)

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Septal perforation is not seen in: [DNB 02]
questions.explanation: Rhinophyma is hypertrophy of sebaceous glands of the tip of nose. It does not cause septal perforation.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Perforation of palate is/are seen with: [PGI Nov 2012]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 151; Scott Brown Otolaryngology 7/e, Vol 2, Chapter 124, p 1583.
Causes of palatal perforation
Developmental: During the sixth week of prenatal period, palatal shelves coalesce to form the hard palate. Failure of this integration results in cleft palate.
Infectious: Leprosy, tertiary syphilis, tuberculosis, rhinoscleroma, naso-oral blastomycosis, leishmaniasis, actinomycosis, histoplasmosis, coccidiomycosis and diphtheria.
Autoimmune: Lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease and Wegener's granulomatosis.
Neoplastic: Different tumors can extend from maxillary sinus or nasal cavity and perforate the palate.
Drug related: Palatal perforation due to cocaine abuse is a well-known situation. Other drugs (heroine, narcotics) can be responsible for palatal perforation.
Iatrogenic: Sometimes following a tooth extraction an oro-antral fistula remains. Other procedures such as tumor surgery (maxillectomy), corrective surgeries (e.g. septoplasty) or intubation can cause palatal perforation.
Rare causes: Rhinolith can result in palatal perforation.
Note: Aphthous ulcers involve soft palate whereas spare the mucosa of hard palate and gingivae.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: The etiology of anterior ethmoidal neuralgia is: [AIIMS 03]

options.text: Inferior turbinate pressing on the nasal septum
Middle turbinate pressing on the nasal septum
Superior turbinate pressing on the nasal septum

questions.answerText: Middle turbinate pressing on the nasal septum
questions.explanation:
Ref. Turner 10/e, p 66; Dhingra 6/e, p 449.
Sluder's neuralgia or the anterior ethmoidal syndrome is pain around the bridge of the nose radiating into the forehead. It is said to originate from the middle turbinate (part of ethmoid bone) pressing on the deviated septum. This is a rare cause of headache and also k/a contact point headache.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Cottle's test tests the patency of the nares in: [JIPMER]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 149; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 287.
Cottle test: It is used to test nasal obstruction due to abnormality of nasal valve as in case of deviated nasal septum.
In this test, cheek is drawn laterally while the patient breathes quietly. If the nasal airway improves on the test side, the test is positive, and indicates abnormality of the vestibular component of nasal valve.
Also Know: Other tests for checking patency of nasal cavities
Spatula test
Cotton wool test
Various Tests of ENT
Test
Condition
ABLB test of Fowler
To test positive recruitment as in Meniere's disease and presbycusis
Bing test and Chimani-Moos test
Tuning fork test to detect hearing loss
Doerfler-Stewart test
To detect malingering
Erhard's test
Gault's test
Crowe-Beck test
Done in lateral sinus thrombosis
Tobey-Ayer test (Queckenstedt's)
Done in lateral sinus thrombosis

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: Most common location of nasal hemangioma: [PGI May 2013]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Textbook of ENT, Hazarika 3/e, p 371.
Nasal Hemangiomas:
Hemangioma and angioma are common in nasal septum.
It can also arise from turbinates, nasopharynx and rarely external nose (nasal tip is M/C site in external nose).
M/C features – Nasal obstruction and epistaxis.
Management – Laser excision.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: After laparoscopic appendicectomy, patient had fall from bed on her nose after which she had swelling in nose and difficulty in breathing. Next step in management: [AIIMS May 2013, 07]

options.text: Discharge after 2 days and follow up of the patient after 8 weeks

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 150.
She has possibly developed septal hematoma. A septal hematoma has to be drained as early as possible (Generally within 72 hrs) or else it can lead to necrosis of septal cartilage and loss of support of dorsum leading to saddling of nose. It can also get infected and lead to formation of septal abscess.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 16: Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum
questions.stem: A 2 year old child is brought to the hospital with a compressible swelling at the root of nose, most likely diagnosis is: [AIIMS 1999]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Read below.
Two year child with compressible swelling at the root of nose is most likely a Meningoencephalocele.
Lacrimal sac cyst occurs as a compressible swelling near the medial canthus and not root of nose.
Ethmoid cyst (mucocele) presents as a swelling at the medial quadrant of orbit pushing the orbit forwards and laterally.
AV malformation is a congenital abnormal connection between arteries and veins, bypassing the capillary system. These are largely found in internal organs and is rare at this site.
END OF CHAPTER 16 MCQs
This completes Chapter 16 (Diseases of External Nose and Nasal Septum) with all MCQs, explanations, and relevant theory content integrated. The chapter now covers:
Saddle Nose - Depressed nasal dorsum, Causes (HOT SALT mnemonic: Hematoma, Operative, Trauma, Syphilis, Abscess, Leprosy, Tuberculosis), Management (Augmentation rhinoplasty)
Crooked/Deviated Nose - Humped nose, Crooked nose (dorsum deviated but tip in midline), Deviated nose (both dorsum and tip deviated)
Choanal Atresia - Persistence of bucconasal membrane, Right side > Left side, Unilateral > Bilateral, B/L presents with respiratory obstruction in newborn, Diagnosis (Mucoid discharge, Absence of air bubbles, Failure to pass catheter, Methylene blue dye test, CT scan), Treatment (McGovern's technique for B/L, Definitive correction at 1½ years, Mitomycin C to prevent restenosis), CHARGE syndrome
Tumors of External Nose - Congenital (Dermoid, Encephalocele, Glioma, Nasoalveolar cyst), Benign (Rhinophyma, Papilloma, Hemangioma, Pigmented nevus, Seborrheic keratosis, Neurofibroma, Tumors of sweat glands), Malignant (Basal cell carcinoma - M/C, Squamous cell carcinoma - 2nd M/C, Melanoma)
Rhinophyma/Potato Tumor - Hypertrophy of sebaceous glands, Acne rosacea, Men past middle age, Pink lobulated mass, Treatment (CO2 laser, Shaving, Dermabrasion, Skin grafting)
Nasal Encephalocele - Herniation of glial tissues and meninges, Foramen cecum defect, M/C location occipital then frontal, Positive Furstenberg test, IOC = MRI, First investigation = CT scan, Treatment (Transnasal endoscopic excision), Never do biopsy (CSF rhinorrhea risk)
Nasal Glioma - Heterotopic brain tissue, No intracranial connection, 60% extranasal, 30% intranasal, 10% combined, Firm and noncompressible, Furstenberg test negative, Treatment (Surgical excision)
Dermoid - Ectodermal cyst, Midline over dorsum of nose, Fluctuating cystic swelling, Compressible and nonexpansible, Treatment (Excision)
Deviated Nasal Septum (DNS) - M/C cause: Birth trauma, Types (Anterior dislocation, C-shaped, S-shaped, Spurs), Symptoms, Cottle test, Treatment (Septoplasty - preferred, SMR - Killian incision, Freer's incision for septoplasty), Surgery after 17 years
Septal Perforation - Etiology (Trauma - M/C, Chronic inflammation, Nasal myiasis, Rhinolith, Poisons, Tumors, Idiopathic), Syphilis causes bony perforation, Lupus/TB/Leprosy cause cartilaginous perforation, Symptoms (Whistling sound, Crusts), Treatment (Small/medium - surgical closure, Large - Obturators/Silastic buttons)
Septal Hematoma - Collection of blood under mucoperichondrium, Etiology (Trauma, Septal surgery, Bleeding disorders), Clinical features (B/L nasal obstruction, Soft fluctuant swelling), Treatment (Aspiration for small, Incision and drainage for large), Complications (Thickened septum, Septal abscess → saddle nose)
Septal Abscess - Leads to septal perforation, saddle nose deformity, meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis

questions.stem: Samter's triad includes:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7th/ed Vol 2, p 1472; Internet search – wikipedia.org; Textbook of Mohan Bansal, p 307.
Samter's triad is a medical condition consisting of asthma, aspirin sensitivity, and nasal/ethmoidal polyposis. It occurs in middle age (twenties and thirties are the most common onset times) and may not include any allergies.
Most commonly, the first symptom is rhinitis.
The disorder typically progresses to asthma, then polyposis, with aspirin sensitivity coming last.
The aspirin reaction can be severe, including an asthma attack, anaphylaxis, and urticaria in some cases. Patients typically react to other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, although paracetamol is generally considered safe.
Anosmia (lack of smell) is also typical, as the inflammation reaches the olfactory receptors in the nose.

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 159; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 317.
Mucormycosis is fungal infection of nose and paranasal sinuses which may prove rapidly fatal if untreated. It is seen in uncontrolled diabetes or in those taking immunosuppressive drugs. It presents as black necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate. Treatment is by amphotericin B and surgical debridement.
NOTE: Most common fungal infection of nose is Aspergillosis.

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 156; Scott Brown's 7/e, Vol 2 Chapter 115, p 1462, 1463; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 315.
Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by gram-negative Frisch bacteria Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis.
Pathologically:
Mikulicz cells or foam cells and Russell bodies are its characteristic features.
Russell bodies are homogenous eosinophilic inclusion bodies found in plasma cells.
In a patient presenting with atrophic dry nasal mucosa, extensive crusting and woody hard external nose: Rhinoscleroma should be suspected.

questions.stem: About nasal syphilis the following is true: [PGI 02]

options.text: In newborn, it presents as snuffles
Secondary syphilis is the common association

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 157.
Nasal syphilis may be:
Acquired:
Primary, e.g. chancre in vestibule
Secondary, e.g. simple rhinitis, crusting and fissuring leading to atrophic rhinitis
Tertiary, e.g. Gumma leads to septal perforation and saddle nose deformity (due to collapse of nasal bridge)
Congenital:
Early (first 3 months): Presenting as snuffles, purulent nasal discharge, fissuring excoriation.
Late (around puberty): Gumma in septum and other stigmata.
Tertiary syphilis is a common association: primary and secondary syphilis are rare association in nasal syphilis. Septal perforation occurs in bony part in case of syphilis.

questions.stem: Antrochoanal polyp is characterized by: [PGI Dec 03]

options.text: Caldwell-Luc operation is treatment of choice in recurrent cases

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 174, 175; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2 Chapter 121, p 1554; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 308, 309.
Nasal polyps are non-neoplastic masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. They do not bleed on touch and are insensitive to probing and never present with epistaxis or bleeding from nose. Recurrence is uncommon in case of antrochoanal polyp. Antrochoanal polyps arise from maxillary antrum and then grow into choana and nasal cavity.

questions.stem: A patient presents with antrochoanal polyp arising from the medial wall of the maxilla. Which of the following would be the best management for the patient? [AIIMS May 2014]
questions.explanation: Current treatment of choice of antrochoanal polyp is endoscopic sinus surgery, which has superseded other modes of polyp removal. In this procedure, all polyps are removed under endoscopic control especially from the key area of the osteomeatal complex. This procedure helps to preserve the normal function of the sinuses. FESS can be done under local anesthesia although general anesthesia is preferred.

questions.stem: The current treatment of choice for a large antrochoanal polyp in a 30-year-old man is: [AIIMS Nov 05]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 175; Maqbool 11/e, p 206.
FESS is Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery.
Current treatment of choice of antrochoanal polyp is endoscopic sinus surgery which has superseded other modes of polyp removal in all age groups.
In this procedure all polyps are removed under endoscopic control especially from the key area of the osteomeatal complex. This procedure helps to preserve the normal function of the sinuses. FESS can be done under local anesthesia although general anesthesia is preferred.
Caldwell-Luc operation is avoided these days.

questions.explanation: Ethmoidal polyps are mostly seen in adults (30-60 years). They are rarely seen in childhood. They are only seen in childhood in association with mucoviscidosis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose
questions.stem: Recurrent polyps are seen in: [UP 07]
questions.explanation:
Mohan Bansal, p 308.
Ethmoidal Polyps
They are mostly seen in adults.
Etiology – usual cause of ethmoidal polyps is allergy.
"Allergic nasal polyps are rarely, if ever seen in childhood. They are only seen in childhood in association with mucoviscidosis." - Turner 10/e, p 373.
Ethmoidal polyps are also associated with:
Bronchial asthma
Aspirin intolerance
Cystic fibrosis
Nasal mastocytosis
Syndromes like: Kartagener's/Young syndrome/Churg-Strauss syndrome
Mnemonic: Adult B M R
Adult - It is seen in adults
B = Bilateral
M = Multiple
R = Recurrence is common

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose
questions.stem: In a patient with multiple bilateral nasal polyps with X-ray showing opacity in the paranasal sinuses. The treatment consists of all of the following except: [AIIMS 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 173; Turner 10/e, p 52, 54.
This patient is having ethmoidal polyp (because polyps are multiple and bilateral). Main etiology of polyps is allergy.
Medical treatment of polyps is the same as that for allergic rhinitis which consists of:
Antihistaminics
Steroids - helpful in patients who cannot tolerate antihistamine or have asthma along with polyps. It is also useful to prevent recurrence after surgery.
Decongestants such as epinephrine, phenylephrine, xylometazoline, etc.
Antifungals (e.g. Amphotericin B) have no role in treatment of polyps.

questions.chapter: Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose
questions.stem: Patient with ethmoidal polyp undergoes polypectomy. Presents 6 months later with ethmoidal polyp. Correct Rx: [AIIMS 95]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 173.
Treatment of ethmoidal polyp
Simple polypectomy: When there are one or two pedunculated polyps.
Intranasal ethmoidectomy: Indicated when polyps are multiple and sessile.
Extranasal ethmoidectomy: This is indicated when polyps recur after intranasal procedures.
Transantral ethmoidectomy: Indicated when infection and polypoidal changes are also seen in the maxillary antrum. In this case antrum is opened by Caldwell-Luc approach and the ethmoidal air cells approached through the medial wall of the antrum.
NOTE: These days, ethmoidal polypi are removed by endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) which is the TOC.

questions.chapter: Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose
questions.stem: "Bernoulli's theorem" explains: [UP 07]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Textbook of ENT, Hazarika 3/e, p 343.
Bernoulli's theorem states that as velocity of air increases, lateral pressure decreases. More the velocity, more is the drop in lateral pressure. When air passes through nasal valve area—narrowest part, the velocity of air increases, which leads to drop in pressure such that negative pressure occurs. This negative pressure facilitates accumulation of edematous fluid in the submucosa leading to polyp formation.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose

questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott-Brown 7/e, p 1553; Turner 10/e, p 55.
Topical steroids are not recommended in post surgery for antrochoanal polyps.
For antrochoanal polyps, cause is infection and not the allergy. Antrochoanal polyps are single, unilateral and rarely recur. Topical steroids are rarely recommended.

questions.stem: About foreign body in a child true statement is: [PGI June 03]

options.text: Inanimate is more common than animate

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 161; Turner 10/e, p 62; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1, p 1186.
Foreign Bodies in Children can be:
Animate: Examples are screwworms, larvae, maggots and black carpet beetles.
Inanimate: These are more common. Examples are peas, beans, dried pulses, nuts, paper, cotton wool and pieces of pencil.
Clinical Features
Unilateral foul smelling discharge in a child is pathognomonic of a foreign body.
It can lead to vestibulitis.
Treatment
Removal with forceps or blunt hook under LA.
Indications of giving GA in Nasal Foreign Body Removal
Uncooperative or very apprehensive child
Troublesome bleeding if the foreign body is firmly embedded in granulation tissue
Posteriorly placed foreign body.
If a foreign body is strongly suspected but can't be found.

questions.stem: Most common cause of U/L mucopurulent rhinorrhea in a child is: [Kolkata 01/FMGE 2013]

questions.explanation:

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose
questions.stem: A child has retained disc battery in the nose. What is the most important consideration in the management? [AIIMS Nov, 14]

options.text: Battery substance leaks and cause tissue damage

questions.answerText: Battery substance leaks and cause tissue damage
questions.explanation:
Ref: Dhingra 6/e, p 161; Scott-Brown 7/e, p 1186; Turner 10/e, p 62.
Most important consideration in the management of retained disc battery in the nose of a child is the leakage of battery substance leading to tissue damage.
"If the FB is a small button battery, moisture within the cavity may lead to tissue damage. Irrigation or nasal wash should not be used. If the battery leaks, there may be liquefactive necrosis and organ injury. It should be removed immediately." - http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/nasal-injury-and-nasal-foreign-bodies Professional Reference.

options.text: Deposition of calcium around foreign body in nose

questions.answerText: Deposition of calcium around foreign body in nose
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 161; Tuli 1/e, p 149; Scott-Brown 7/e, Vol 1, p 1186; Textbook of Mohan Bansal, p 349.
Rhinoliths are calcareous masses which result due to deposition of salts like calcium and magnesium carbonates and phosphates around the nucleus of a foreign body.
For more details, see text part.

questions.chapter: Chapter 17: Granulomatous Disorders of Nose, Nasal Polyps and Foreign Body in Nose

questions.stem: Maggots in the nose are best treated by: [AI 98; 96]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 162.
Chloroform water or vapor must be instilled in order to anesthetize or kill the maggots and so release their grip from the skin.
Maggots are larval forms of flies, particularly of the genus Chrysomyia.
Patient may present as a simple case of epistaxis.
Maggots cause extensive destruction of nose, sinuses, soft tissues of face, palate or around the nose.
Death may occur from meningitis.
END OF CHAPTER 17 MCQs
Granulomatous Diseases - Classification (Bacterial, Fungal, Unspecified)
Lupus Vulgaris - Indolent TB infection, Apple-jelly nodules, Butterfly appearance, Perforation of cartilaginous septum, ATT
Syphilis - Primary (Chancre), Secondary (Rhinitis/crusting), Tertiary (Gumma, septal perforation, saddle nose), Congenital (Snuffles), Bony perforation
Rhinoscleroma (Mikulicz Disease) - Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (Frisch bacillus), Stages (Atrophic, Granulomatous, Cicatricial), Mikulicz cells, Russell bodies, Hebra nose, Tapir nose, Treatment (Streptomycin + Tetracycline)
Leprosy - Lepromatous leprosy, Nasal septum (anterior part), Inferior turbinate, Saddle nose, Dapsone/INH/Rifampin
Rhinosporidiosis - Rhinosporidium seeberi (Protozoa), Strawberry/pink-purple polypoidal mass, White dots (sporangia), Endemic in India, Treatment (Excision + Cautery at base, Dapsone)
Aspergillosis - A. fumigatus (90%), Black/grayish membrane, Fungal ball in maxillary sinus, Surgical debridement + Antifungals
Mucormycosis - Aggressive opportunistic infection, Uncontrolled diabetes, Black necrotic mass, Affinity for blood vessels, Amphotericin B, Surgical debridement, Orbital exenteration
Nasal Polyps - Non-neoplastic, Soft/fleshy/pale, Insensitive to pain, Do not shrink with vasoconstrictors, Do not bleed
Ethmoidal Polyps - Adults (30-60 years), B/L, Multiple, Allergy (M/C), Associated with bronchial asthma, Samter's triad (Asthma, Aspirin intolerance, Nasal polyps), Treatment (Medical: Intranasal steroids; Surgical: Polypectomy, Intranasal ethmoidectomy, Extranasal ethmoidectomy, FESS)
Antrochoanal Polyps (Killian's Polyp) - Children/young adults, U/L, Arises from maxillary antrum, Allergy + Infection, Treatment (Intranasal polypectomy for children, Caldwell-Luc for recurrence in >17 years, FESS current TOC)
Bernoulli's Phenomenon - Explains nasal polyp formation (Negative pressure at stenotic site facilitates fluid accumulation)
Foreign Bodies in Nose - Children, Unilateral foul smelling discharge (pathognomonic), Inanimate > Animate, Disc battery (Leakage causes tissue damage), Parent's Kiss technique, Rhinolith (Calcium deposition around foreign body), Nasal myiasis (Chloroform water)
Caldwell-Luc Operation - Nasoantral window through inferior meatus, M/C complication: Infraorbital nerve palsy (21%)

questions.chapter: Chapter 18: Inflammatory Disorders of Nasal Cavity
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 18: Inflammatory Disorders of Nasal Cavity
questions.stem: Early mediators of allergic rhinitis are: [PGI 03]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Robbin's 7/e, p 208, 209; Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 267, 268; Dhingra 6/e, p 167.
Allergic rhinitis is Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction.
Pathology
In individuals who have genetic predisposition to allergy → Allergen exposure leads to IgE antibody production → Attaches to mast cell (by Fc end). On subsequent exposure to the same allergen → It attaches itself to IgE antibody (which in turn is attached to mast cell) by its Fab end → Degranulation of mast cell → Release of mediators like histamine, leukotriene, cytokines, prostaglandins, platelet activating factor → Called as Early phase/Humoral reaction.
Early phase occurs within 10-15 mins (max 30 mins) of allergen exposure.
It is due to release of mediators viz. histamine, cytokine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, platelet activating factor.
Release of histamine causes symptoms like – sneezing, rhinorrhea, itching, vascular permeability, vasodilatation, glandular secretion.
Release of cytokines and leukotrienes in the early phase causes influx of inflammatory cells (eosinophils) → Called as later phase of cellular reaction.
Occurs 2-8 hours after initial sensitization.
Causes symptoms like Nasal congestion and postnasal drip.

questions.stem: All of the following surgical procedures are used for allergic rhinitis except: [AIIMS 04]

options.text: Radiofrequency ablation of the inferior turbinate
Laser ablation of the inferior turbinate
Submucosal placement of silastic in inferior turbinate

questions.answerText: Submucosal placement of silastic in inferior turbinate
questions.explanation:
Ref. Turner 10/e, p 39, 53; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, Chapter 104, p 1400, 1401.
Surgery is done in a case of allergic rhinitis when other methods have failed or when there is marked septal deviation or bony turbinate enlargement which makes topical nasal spray usage difficult. It should never be used as first line of treatment.
Surgery:
To relieve nasal obstruction: Turbinate reduction or turbinate resection is done by either diathermy—to fibrose, the vascular spaces of inferior turbinates, Cryosurgery, Laser cautery, Radiofrequency ablation or turbinectomy.
To relieve rhinorrhea: Vidian neurectomy is done.
NOTE: Submucosal injection of teflon or placement of silastic is the treatment option for Atrophic rhinitis where we need to make nasal cavity more roomy.

questions.chapter: Chapter 18: Inflammatory Disorders of Nasal Cavity
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 18: Inflammatory Disorders of Nasal Cavity
questions.stem: All are implicated in etiology of atrophic rhinitis except: [DNB 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 153.
Atrophic Rhinitis
Primary
Secondary
The exact etiology is not known. It can be due to: H = Hereditary factors; E = Endocrinal disturbance because it starts at puberty and ceases after menopause. Female > Male; R = Racial factors – White and Yellow races are susceptible; N = Nutritional deficiency of Vit A, D and iron; I = Infective (organisms like Klebsiella ozaenae, diphtheroids, P. vulgaris, E. coli, Staphylococci, Streptococci); A = Autoimmune process
Secondary rhinitis can be due to: Specific infections like Syphilis, Leprosy, Rhinoscleroma; Longstanding purulent sinusitis; Radiotherapy to nose; Surgical removal of turbinates
NOTE: DNS can lead to unilateral atrophic rhinitis on the wider side.

questions.explanation:

Atrophic rhinitis: We have done in detail in text. Here just remember:
It is more common in females.
Age—Usually starts at puberty and ceases after menopause.
It is always bilateral except in case of DNS where atrophic rhinitis is seen on the wider side.
Young's operation (closure of both nostrils) is done for atrophic rhinitis to reduce the size of roomy nasal cavities.

questions.chapter: Chapter 18: Inflammatory Disorders of Nasal Cavity
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 18: Inflammatory Disorders of Nasal Cavity
questions.stem: Vidian neurectomy is done in: [CUPGEE 97]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 170; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1412.
Excessive rhinorrhea in vasomotor rhinitis not corrected by medical therapy and bothersome to the patient, is relieved by sectioning the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to nose, i.e. vidian neurectomy.
NOTE: The parasympathetic/secretomotor supply of the nose comes through the vidian nerve (also called the nerve of pterygoid canal). It is formed by greater superficial petrosal branch of facial nerve joining deep petrosal nerve derived from plexus around internal carotid artery (sympathetic nerve supply).

END OF CHAPTER 18 MCQs
Classification of Rhinitis - Acute (Acute Rhinitis, Acute nasal diphtheria), Chronic (Specific, Nonspecific, Allergic)
Acute Rhinitis/Coryza - Common cold, Rhinovirus (M/C), Secondary invaders, Clinical features (Burning/tickling, Rhinorrhea, Sneezing, Nasal stuffiness), Treatment
Hypertrophic Rhinitis - Sequelae of simple rhinitis, Thickening of mucosa/submucosa/seromucinous glands/periosteum/bone, Mulberry appearance, Treatment (Turbinectomy - Laser, Submucosal diathermy, Cryosurgery, SMR of turbinate bone)
Atrophic Rhinitis/Ozaena - Progressive atrophy of nasal mucosa and underlying bone, Excessive crusting, Etiology (Hereditary, Endocrinal, Racial, Nutritional, Infective - Klebsiella ozaenae, Autoimmune), Pathology (Everything atrophies), Clinical features (Merciful anosmia, Nasal obstruction due to crusts, Epistaxis), Signs (Roomy nasal cavities with greenish crusts, Pale mucosa due to obliterative endarteritis, Septal perforation, Saddle deformity, Atrophic pharyngitis/laryngitis), Investigations (X-ray PNS - Water's view), Treatment (Medical: Warm nasal alkaline solution - BBC, 25% glucose in glycerin, Kemicetine antiozaena solution, Potassium iodide, Human placental extract; Surgical: Young's operation, Modified Young's operation, Lautenslager's operation)
Rhinitis Sicca - Hot, dry, dusty surroundings (Iron smith, Bakery workers), Anterior 1/3rd of nose affected, Squamous metaplasia, Treatment (Correction of occupational surroundings, Antibiotic and steroid ointment, Nasal douching)
Allergic Rhinitis - IgE mediated Type I hypersensitivity, Types (Seasonal - Pollens, Perennial - House dust/perfumes/drugs), Clinical features (Itching, Sneezing, Profuse watery discharge, Nasal obstruction), Signs (Pale/boggy mucosa, Allergic salute, Allergic shiners, Dennis Morgan lines), Investigations (Blood - Eosinophilia, Nasal smear, Skin tests - Prick test preferred, RAST), Treatment (Avoidance, Antihistaminics, Corticosteroids, Decongestants, Immunotherapy), Contraindications to immunotherapy
Vasomotor Rhinitis - Non-allergic, Parasympathetic overactivity, Emotionally unstable women (20-40 years), Paroxysmal sneezing, Excessive clear rhinorrhea, Nasal mucosa normal and shining, Hypertrophic turbinates, No eye symptoms, Treatment (Medical: Avoidance, Decongestants, Steroids; Surgical: Vidian neurectomy, Anticholinergics - Ipratropium bromide, Azelastine spray)
Rhinitis Caseosa/Nasal Cholesteatoma - Chronic inflammation, Offensive cheesy material, U/L, Males > Females, Treatment (Removal of debris, Repeated irrigation)
Rhinitis Medicamentosa - Excessive use of topical decongestants, Rebound congestion, Treatment (Withdrawal of offending drug, Short course of systemic and local steroids)
