questions.stem: Causes of epistaxis are all except:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 176, 167; TB of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 294.
Amongst the options given, foreign body, tumor, hypertension all can lead to epistaxis.
Remember: Many nasal problems can lead to epistaxis viz nasal trauma, viral rhinitis, chronic infections of nose (which lead to crust formation like atrophic rhinitis, rhinitis sicca, TB of nose), foreign bodies in nose (maggots and non living), DNS, neoplasms (hemangioma, papilloma, carcinoma or sarcoma).
Two nasal conditions which do not lead to epistaxis:
Nasal polyps
Allergic rhinitis
Pharyngeal conditions which lead to epistaxis:
Adenoiditis
Juvenile angiofibroma
Malignant tumors

Little area (also called as Kiesselbach's plexus) is a highly vascular area in the anteroinferior part of nasal septum just above the vestibule. It is the most common site for nasal bleeding as this area is exposed to the drying effect of inspiratory current and to finger nail trauma.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: M/C cause of epistaxis in 3 years old child: [PGI 98]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1, p 1064.
Friends – I know some of you must be thinking foreign body as the answer but it is not the most common cause.
M/C cause of epistaxis in children is idiopathic.2nd M/C cause of epistaxis in children is Infection/Trauma → Development of crusts → Nasal picking/Digital trauma → Nasal bleed.
Still if you have doubt read the following lines of Scotts Brown:
"Epistaxis – Children are especially susceptible to nose bleeds due to extensive vascular supply to nasal mucosa and the frequency with which they develop upper respiratory tract infections." Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1, p 1063.
"Epistaxis is more common in children with upper respiratory allergies." Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1, p 1063.
"There is a seasonal variation with a higher prevalence in the winter months perhaps due to the greater frequency of upper respiratory tract infections." Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1, p 1063.

questions.stem: Recurrent epistaxis in a 15-year-old female the most common cause is: [JIPMER 90]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Read Below.
As such this answer is not given anywhere but we can come to the correct answer by exclusion.
Option "a" is Juvenile nasopharyngeal fibroma. It is seen in adolescent males and is therefore the most common cause of recurrent epistaxis in males and not in females. Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 346.
Option "b" is Rhinosporidiosis is a cause of epistaxis but usually occurs in young males from India. Ref. Turner 10/e, p 61.
Option "c" is Foreign body which is a cause of epistaxis in children and is not commonly seen in 15 years of age.
So we are left with hematopoietic disorder which can be seen in a 15 years old female. Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 161.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: Diagnosis in a 10-year-old boy with recurrent epistaxis and a unilateral nasal mass is: [SGPGI 05]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 246. Recurrent epistaxis in a 10-year-old boy with unilateral nasal mass is diagnostic of juvenile nasopharyngeal fibroma. For details, see chapter on Pharyngeal Tumor.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: Epistaxis in elderly person is common in: [AI 04]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Maqbool 11/e, p 180; Textbook of Mohan Bansal, p 295.
According to Scott Brown 7th/ed Vol 2 p 1600 – M/C cause of adult epistaxis is idiopathic though a number of factors increase its chances like use of NSAIDs and alcohol. It further says there is no proven association between hypertension and adult Epistaxis, but still "Elevated blood pressure is observed in almost all epistaxis admissions. This apparent hypertension in acute admissions may be a result of anxiety associated with hospital admission and the invasive techniques used to control the bleeding." Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 167.
But still the answer to this question is hypertension by ruling out other options:
Option a – foreign body – is a cause of epistaxis in children and not in elderly age group.
Option b – allergic rhinitis – does not lead to epistaxis. Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 181.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma does cause epistaxis and is seen in elderly age group but is not the most common cause as in itself nasopharyngeal carcinoma is not common.
"Nasal tumors seldom present as epistaxis in isolation Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma and hemangiopericytoma are rare vascular tumors which can present with severe or recurrent epistaxis in association with nasal obstruction." Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 263.
Hence our answer by exclusion is hypertension. The answer is further supported by Maqbool 11th/ed p 180 which says: "Hypertension is a very common disease and causes epistaxis frequently in elderly patients."

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: Systemic causes of epistaxis are all except: [UP 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1605.
Epistaxis in Adult
Primary
Secondary
No cause is identified but may be due to: Use of NSAIDs, Use of alcohol, Hypertension (role not proven)
Cause is identified and it is due to: Coagulopathy secondary to liver disease/kidney disease/leukemia or myelosuppression, Trauma, Post surgery like inferior turbinectomy, Endoscopic sinus surgery, Warfarin intake (anticoagulant treatment), Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
Hemophilia is a Secondary Cause of Epistaxis in Children. Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1, p 1065. Hence the answer is d i.e. hemophilia which is not a cause of secondary epistaxis but is implicated in the etiology of primary epistaxis though its role is doubted there also.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: A 70 years aged patient with epistaxis, patient is hypertensive with BP = 200/100 mm Hg. On examination no active bleeding noted, next step of management is:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1, p 1065.
We do not need any reference to answer this particular question as the answer is hidden in the question only. The question itself says that no active bleeding is seen—so no need to do anything just observe the patient and because his B/P is 200/100 mm Hg which is quite high, give him antihypertensive drugs.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: Source of epistaxis after ligation of external carotid artery is: [AIIMS 93]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 178; TB of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 35; Scott Brown 7/e Vol 2, p 1599.
Nose is Supplied by
Internal carotid artery
External carotid artery
Anterior ethmoidal artery; Posterior ethmoidal artery
Facial Artery: Superior labial artery; Maxillary artery: Greater palatine artery, Branches of sphenopalatine artery (nasopalatine, post nasal septal branches and posterior lateral nasal branches), Anterior superior dental artery
In the Question: Greater palatine artery, Superior labial artery, Maxillary artery are all branches of external carotid artery. If external carotid artery is ligated, the source of epistaxis will be ethmoidal artery which is a branch of Internal carotid artery.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: If posterior epistaxis cannot be controlled, which artery is ligated: [Kolkata 00]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1603, 1606.
Ligation technique is reserved for intractable bleeding where the source cannot be located or controlled by other techniques. The hierarchy of arteries used for ligation is:
Sphenopalatine artery
Internal maxillary artery
External carotid Artery
Anterior/posterior ethmoidal artery
Earlier the most common artery ligated was maxillary artery but now endonasal sphenopalatine artery ligation (ESPAL) is the ligation of choice.
"ESPAL is the current ligation of choice controlling bleeding in over 90% of cases with a low complication rate." Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1606.
Transnasal Endonasal Sphenopalatine Ligation (TESPAL or ESPAL)
It is the most popular procedure for ligation and has replaced internal maxillary artery ligation.
Can be done under LA/GA
Incision is given 8 mm anterior and under the posterior end of middle turbinate
Sphenopalatine artery is ligated in the sphenopalatine foramen
Success rate ~100%
Complications very rare – rebleeding, infection and nasal adhesions
Internal Maxillary Artery Ligation
Earlier it was the ligation procedure of choice for uncontrolled bleeding:
Internal maxillary artery is ligated in the pterygopalatine fossa using a Caldwell-Luc approach (3rd part of the artery is ligated)
Success rate – 89%
Complications – Sinusitis, damage to infraorbital nerve, oroantral fistula, dental damage and anesthesia, and rarely ophthalmoplegia and blindness.
External carotid artery ligation and anterior and posterior ethmoidal artery ligation is not commonly done.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: In case of uncontrolled epistaxis, ligation of internal maxillary artery is to be done in the: [Kolkata 01]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1603; Textbook of Mohan Bansal, p 296.
Ligation of
Site
Sphenopalatine artery
Sphenopalatine foramen
Internal maxillary artery
Pterygopalatine fossa
External carotid artery
Above the origin of superior thyroid artery
Ethmoidal arteries
Between inner canthus of eye and midline of nose

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: Treatment of choice in recurrent epistaxis in a patient with hereditary hemotelangiectasis: [Kolkota 05]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 180; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1605; Textbook of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 297.
Hereditary hemotelangiectasia (HHT) or Osler-Weber-Rendu disease is an autosomal dominant condition affecting blood vessels in the skin, mucous membranes and viscera. The genetic abnormality is located to chromosome 9 and 12.
Classical features:
Telangiectasia
A/V malformations
Aneurysms
Recurrent epistaxis (seen in 93% cases)
Management:
Medical: Estrogen therapy, Aminocaproic acid
Surgical: KTP or Nd YAG Laser; Septodermoplasty (This is the treatment of choice in recurrent epistaxis in HHT); Embolization

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: Kiesselbach's plexus is situated on the: [DNB 2005, 11]

options.text: Medial wall of the middle ear
Medial wall of the nasal cavity

questions.answerText: Medial wall of the nasal cavity
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 176.
Kiesselbach's plexus is situated in the anterior inferior part of nasal septum (which forms the medial wall of nose) just above the vestibule.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 19: Epistaxis
questions.stem: Posterior epistaxis occurs from: [Kerala 2010]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 450. Woodruff's plexus is a venous plexus situated inferior to the posterior end of inferior turbinate. It is the site of posterior epistaxis in adults.
END OF CHAPTER 19 MCQs
Definition - Bleeding from inside the nose
Areas of Nasal Bleed - Little's area (M/C site in children and young adults, Anteroinferior part of nasal septum, Kiesselbach's plexus, Arteries contributing: Sphenopalatine/artery of epistaxis, Anterior ethmoidal, Septal branch of greater palatine, Septal branch of superior labial), Retrocolumellar vein (Venous bleeding in young people <35 yrs), Woodruff's plexus (Lateral nasal wall inferior to posterior end of inferior turbinate, Venous plexus, Posterior epistaxis, Browne's area)
Classification - Anterior vs Posterior (Scott Brown), Childhood (<16 years) vs Adult (>16 years), Primary (Idiopathic, 70-80%) vs Secondary (Defined cause)
Epistaxis in Children - Common, innocuous, Rare <2 years, Peak 3-8 years, Winter months, M/C site: Anterior part of nasal septum, M/C site of bleeding: Little's area, M/C cause: Idiopathic, 2nd M/C: Digital trauma/Nose picking, Unilateral epistaxis → Rule out foreign body
Causes of Recurrent Epistaxis in Children - Allergic rhinitis, Retained nasal foreign body, Intranasal steroid sprays, Hemorrhagic disease (ITP, von Willebrand disease), Vascular abnormalities (A/V malformations, Hemangioma), Angiofibroma (Adolescent boys), Nasal parasitosis/mycosis
Adult Recurrent Epistaxis - Coagulopathy (Liver/kidney disease, leukemia, myelosuppression), Trauma, Post surgery, Warfarin, Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, Tumors (Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, hemangiopericytoma)
Table 19.1 - Anterior vs Posterior Epistaxis (Incidence, Site, Age, Cause, Bleeding severity)
Management - First-aid (Nasal pinching, Ice packs, Trotter's method), Hospital (Sedation - Pethidine), Anterior Nasal Packing (Ribbon gauze with Neosporin, Merocel packs, Balloon tamponade), Posterior Nasal Packing (Cardiovascular complications, Sleep apnea)
Vessel Ligation - Hierarchy (Sphenopalatine/TESPAL, Internal maxillary, External carotid, Anterior/posterior ethmoidal), External carotid ligation (Above superior thyroid artery), Maxillary artery ligation (Pterygopalatine fossa, Caldwell-Luc approach), TESPAL (Ligation of choice, Sphenopalatine foramen, Success rate ~100%), Ethmoidal arteries (Between inner canthus and midline)
Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu Disease) - Autosomal dominant, Chromosome 9 and 12, Telangiectasia, A/V malformations, Aneurysms, Recurrent epistaxis (93%), Treatment (KTP/Nd YAG Laser, Septodermoplasty)

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Antrum of Highmore is:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra ENT 6/e, p 187. Maxillary Sinus is called as antrum of Highmore.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Sinus which is not present at birth:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra ENT 6/e, p 189; TB of ENT, Hazarika 3/e, p 238. Both sphenoid and Frontal sinus are absent at birth, but the last to develop is frontal sinus, hence we are taking it as correct option.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: First paranasal sinus to develop at birth is:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 187. Maxillary sinus is the first sinus to develop after birth.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: The sinus which is most superior in face is:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 187.
The superior most sinus is frontal sinus—as it is located between the inner and outer table of frontal bone, above and deep to supraorbital margin.
This is followed by ethmoid sinus situated between the upper third of lateral nasal wall and medial wall of the orbit.
Next is sphenoid sinus in the body of sphenoid and most inferior is maxillary sinus in the maxillary bone.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: In Water's view which sinus cannot be visualized:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 433.
Sphenoid sinus cannot be visualized with normal water's view. Rest all sinuses can be visualized.
To visualize sphenoid sinus—Water's view with mouth open should be done.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: In Basal view, sinus which can be best seen:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 434. Sphenoid > post-ethmoid > maxillary sinus. This is the order of the sinuses, best seen in basal view.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Best view for frontal sinus:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 434. Best view for frontal sinus is Caldwell-Luc view.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Howarth procedure is related to:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 196. Howarth's or Lynch operation is external frontonasal ethmoidectomy. It is outdated these days.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Antral puncture (proof puncture) is done through:
questions.explanation:
Ref. TB of ENT, Hazarika 3/e, p 311. See text for explanation.
Antral puncture is done by performing antral puncture in inferior meatus with the help of Tilley Lichtwitz trocar and cannula.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Sudden death in case of maxillary wash is due to:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 409. Air embolism is a rare, fatal complication of antral lavage (maxillary wash).

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Proof puncture is done in:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 408. In antral puncture or proof puncture medial wall of maxillary sinus is punctured in the region of inferior meatus for antral lavage.
Indications of proof puncture (Antral lavage):
Chronic and subacute maxillary sinusitis for confirming diagnosis and washing out pus.
To collect specimen in case of suspected malignancy.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Infundibulotomy is done for:
questions.explanation: Ref. TB of ENT Hazarika 3/e, p 332. Infundibulotomy—the uncinate process is removed to open the ethmoidal infundibulum. This is done to approach middle meatus.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Bilateral proptosis and bilateral 6th nerve palsy is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6th/e, p 204. Friends always remember in cavernous sinus thrombosis there is bilateral orbital involvement whereas in orbital cellulitis it is unilateral.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Orbital cellulitis most commonly occurs after which sinus infection:
questions.explanation: Orbital cellulitis occurs most commonly after ethmoid sinusitis as the ethmoid is separated from the orbit by a thin papery bone, the lamina papyracea.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Which of the following is not a complication of sinusitis:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 198 (Table 38.1). See the text for explanation.
Nasal furunculosis is infection of hair follicle in the nasal vestibule. It is not a complication of sinusitis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: In Caldwell-Luc operation the nasoantral window is made through:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 411. In Caldwell-Luc operation the nasoantral window is made through inferior meatus.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Commonest complication of Caldwell-Luc operations is:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 411. Infraorbital nerve injury is the commonest complication of Caldwell-Luc operations.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Caldwell-Luc surgery approach is via:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 411. Caldwell-Luc surgery approach is via sublabial sulcus (canine fossa).

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Nerve injured in Caldwell-Luc surgery is:
questions.explanation: See the text for explanation. Infraorbital nerve injury is the commonest complication of Caldwell-Luc operations.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: In functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) opening is made through:
questions.explanation: See the text for explanation. In FESS = Opening is made via middle meatus. The osteomeatal complex (OMC) is approached moving from anterior to posterior.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Most feared complication of endoscopic sinus surgery is:
questions.explanation: Ref. Operative Otolaryngology H/N Surgery 2/e, chap. 20. The most feared complication of FESS is internal carotid A injury. This is followed by orbital complications.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis · New-pattern question
questions.stem: In nasal endoscopy, eustachian tube is examined at:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 417. Nasal endoscopy for diagnostic purpose—consists of passing a 4 mm 30° endoscope through three passes:
1st pass: To examine through the nasopharynx: Opening of eustachian tube, Walls of nasopharynx, Upper surface of soft palate and uvula, Opening of eustachian tube of opposite side.
2nd pass: It is passed medial to middle turbinate to examine: Sphenoethmoid recess, Superior meatus, Opening of sphenoid sinus, Posterior ethmoidal.
3rd pass: Endoscope is passed to middle meatus to visualize structures of middle meatus in detail.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Which sinus is NOT a part of paranasal sinus? [MP 09]
questions.explanation:
Ref. 6/e, p 187; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 37.
Paranasal sinuses are air containing cavities in certain bones of skull. They are four on each side. Clinically, paranasal sinuses have been divided into two groups.
Anterior group
Posterior group
Maxillary sinus, Frontal sinus, Anterior ethmoidal sinus
Posterior ethmoidal sinus (opens in superior meatus), Sphenoid sinus (opens in sphenoethmoidal recess)
NOTE: All of Anterior group sinuses open in the middle meatus.
Pyriform sinus is a part of hypopharynx, not a paranasal sinus.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: True about sphenoid sinus: [PGI May 2010]

options.text: Present in greater wing of sphenoid

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 188.
All paranasal sinuses are lined by respiratory epithelium (i.e. ciliated pseudo stratified columnar epithelium) i.e. option a is incorrect.
Sphenoid sinus: Important points
It is not present at birth
It occupies the body of sphenoid
Ostium of sphenoid sinus is situated in the upper part of anterior wall and drains into sphenoethmoidal recess.
On x ray: Sphenoid sinus is visible by 4 years of age.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: All are pneumatization patterns of sphenoid sinus except:
questions.explanation:
Three types of sphenoid sinus pneumatisation patterns have been found. Pneumatisation patterns depend on the position of the sinus in relation to the sella turcica (over the body of sphenoid):
a. Conchal: no pneumatisation occurs below the sella. There is a solid block of bone beneath the sella.b. Pre sellar: pneumatisation does not extend beyond the anterior border of sella turcica.c. Sellar/Post sellar: In this case pneumatisation occurs both below and posterior to the sella turcica. This is the most common type of sphenoid pneumatisation seen among individuals.
Concha bullosa is pneumatisation of the middle turbinate, not a sphenoid sinus pneumatization pattern.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Sinus not present at birth is: [Maharashtra 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1320; TB of Mohan Bansal 1/e, p 39.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Pain sensations from the ethmoidal sinus are carried by: [AI 2011]
questions.explanation: As discussed in preceding text, nasociliary nerve—branch of ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve carries pain sensation from ethmoid sinus.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Maxillary sinus achieves maximum size at: [Manipal 06]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Maqbool 11/e, p 148; Turner 10/e, p 9.
Maxillary sinus is the first sinus to develop at birth.
It is completely developed by 9 years of age, i.e. approximately at the time of secondary dentition.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Which among the following sinuses is most commonly affected in a child: [PGI 99]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Tuli 1/e, p 190; Dhingra 6/e, p 193.
Most common sinusitis in children is Ethmoid. Most common sinusitis in adults is Maxillary.
"Ethmoidal sinuses are well developed at birth, hence infants and children below 3 years of age are more likely to have acute ethmoiditis; but after this age, maxillary antral infections are more commonly seen." Ref. Tuli 1/e, p 190.
"Ethmoid sinuses are more often involved in infants and young children." Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 193.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: In acute sinusitis, the sinus most often involved in children is: [UPSC 07]
questions.explanation: Same as above. Most common sinusitis in children is Ethmoid.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Sinus least involved in sinusitis is: [UP 08]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 193; Turner 10/e, p 48.
"Isolated involvement of sphenoid sinus is rare. It is often a part of pansinusitis or is associated with infection of posterior ethmoidal sinus." Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 193.
"The sphenoid sinus is rarely affected on its own" - Turner 10/e, p 48.
The reason for sphenoid sinus to be least affected is that it opens high up in the sphenoethmoid recess which is not affected by most of the conditions of nose.
In Nutshell remember:
M/c sinus affected in adults—Maxillary
M/c sinus affected in children—Ethmoid
Sinus which is least affected—Sphenoid

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Common organisms causing sinusitis: [AI 01]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Harrison 17/e, p 205; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1441; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 299.
"Among community-acquired cases, S. pneumoniae and nontypable Haemophilus influenzae are the most common pathogens, accounting for 50-60% of cases. Moraxella catarrhalis causes disease in a significant percentage (20%) of children but less often in adults. Other streptococcal species and Staphylococcus aureus cause only a small percentage of cases, although there is increasing concern about community strains of methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) as an emerging cause."
According to Nelson 18th/ed, pp 1749, 1750: "The bacterial pathogens causing acute bacterial sinusitis in children and adolescents include Streptococcus pneumoniae (=30%), nontypable Haemophilus influenzae (=20%)."
According to Scotts Brown 7th/ed, p 1441: M/C Organism causing sinusitis in adults is also Streptococcus pneumoniae followed by H. influenza.
In children: M/C is Streptococcus pneumoniae (30-43%) followed by both H. influenza and Moraxella catarrhalis (20-28% each).

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Common organisms causing sinusitis: [PGI 01]
questions.explanation: Same as above.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common etiological agent in paranasal sinus mycoses? [AIIMS May 06]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Maqbool 11/e, p 225; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 1 and 2, p 1452; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 317.
Most common type of fungal infection of nose and paranasal sinuses are due to Aspergillus. A. fumigatus > A. niger > A. flavus are the most frequent offenders.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Which among the following is true regarding fungal sinusitis: [PGI 01]

options.text: Most common organism is Aspergillus niger
Amphoterecin B IV is used for invasive fungal sinusitis
Hazy appearance on X-ray with radiopaque density

questions.explanation:
Ref. Maqbool 11/e, p 225; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1455; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 317, 318.
Most common cause: Aspergillus. Most common species: A. fumigatus (90%) > A. niger > A. flavus. Ref. Maqbool 11/e, p 225.
Other offenders are: Mucor, Rhizopus, Alternaria.
Fungal infection can be of following types:i. Fungus ballii. Allergic fungal rhinosinusitisiii. Chronic or indolent invasive fungal sinusitisiv. Acute fulminant fungal rhinosinusitis
Fungus Ball
Occurs in adult females
M/C agent: Aspergillus
Most common sinus involved – Maxillary > sphenoid sinus
M/C symptom – unilateral postnasal discharge
Most Important Investigation-CT scan
Fungus ball is the main fungal rhinosinusitis in an immunocompetent patient.
Surgery (FESS) is the most effective treatment for fungus ball.
Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis
AFS is a noninvasive fungal rhinosinusitis
Dematiaceous species are the fungal agents mostly responsible for AFRS.
Seen in immunocompetent hosts with allergy to fungus.
Clinical and biological criteria for diagnosis is still under debate, and include nasal polyps, thick mucin, hypersensitivity type I for fungus, eosinophilic mucin.
Sinus opacities with bone extension are frequently seen on CT scan.
Diagnosis of all allergic fungal rhinosinusitis is supported by allergic and fungal criteria.
Treatment = Antifungals
Chronic or Indolent Invasive Fungal Rhinosinusitis
Chronic invasive fungal rhinosinusitis is a rare pathology occurring mostly in immunocompetent patients.
Aspergillus is the most frequent agent isolated in this pathology.
Acute Fulminant Fungal Rhinosinusitis
Fulminant invasive fungal rhinosinusitis occurs in immunocompromised patients (HIV, diabetes, chemotherapy)
Early diagnosis and control of primary immunological disorders is essential for the prognosis.
Thus from the above description it can be concluded:
Option a – Surgery is required for treatment – (correct) as in all forms of fungal sinusitis – some or the other form of surgery is required.
Option b – M/c organism is Aspergillus niger – Incorrect – M/c is A. fumigatus (Maqbool 11/e, p 228).
Option c – Amphotericin IV is used for invasive fungal sinusitis – Correct – Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 210, 6/e, p 196.
Option d – Hazy appearance on X-ray with radiopaque density – Correct – Sinusitis gives hazy appearance on X-ray.
Option e – Seen only in immunodeficient condition – Incorrect – only the acute fulminant form is more common in immunodeficient state whereas others are seen in immunocompetent hosts.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: All of the following are diagnostic criteria of allergic Fungal sinusitis (AFS) except: [AI 08]

options.text: Areas of High attenuation on CT scan

questions.explanation:
Ref. Current Diagnosis and Treatment in Otorhinology 2/e, p 276; Scott Brown 7th/ed Vol 2, p 1452-1454; Ear Nose and Throat Histopathology 2/e, p 152; Patterson's Allergic Disease 6/e, p 778; Allergy and Immunology: An Otolaryngic Approach (2001), p 239.
Allergic fungal sinusitis is a noninvasive form of fungal sinusitis as such orbital invasion is not its feature.
Bent and Kuhn Criteria for Allergic Fungal Sinusitis (AFS)
Type I hypersensitivity (confirmed by history, skin test or serology most important criteria)
Nasal polyposis
Asthma
Unilateral predominance
Eosinophilic mucus demonstrating fungal elements, charcot-leyden crystal
Peripheral eosinophilia
Positive fungal culture
Characteristic Radiological Findings (CT, MRI) absence of tissue invasion by fungus
Radiographic bone erosion
CT scan findings in AFS
Areas of High attenuation surrounded by a thin zone of low attenuation. CT scan reveals pansinusitis and polyposis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Periodicity is a characteristic feature in which sinus infection: [COMED 06]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 192, 193.
Pain of frontal sinusitis shows characteristic periodicity, i.e. comes upon waking, gradually increases and reaches its peak by midday and then starts subsiding. It is also called "office headache" as it is present only during office hours.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Sphenoid sinusitis pain is referred most commonly to: [AP 2005]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra Turner 10/e, p 35; Maqbool 11/e, p 208; Tuli 1/e, p 188.
Acute sphenoiditis: 'Headache – usually localized to the occiput or vertex. Pain may also be referred to the mastoid region.' Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 194.
Also Know: Sinus pain felt in area
Sinus
Pain felt in area
Maxillary sinus
Along the infraorbital margin and referred to upper teeth or gums on affected side (along the distribution of superior orbital nerve). Pain is aggravated on stooping or coughing.
Frontal sinus
Pain localized over forehead. It has a characteristic periodicity.
Ethmoid sinus
Pain localized over the nasal bridge, inner canthus and behind the ear.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Best view for frontal sinus: [AIIMS Nov 2010]
questions.explanation:
Caldwell view is the occipito frontal view. The frontal sinuses are seen clearly in this view.
View
Structure seen
Waters view (with mouth open)
All four sinuses
Schuller's view
Mastoid
Towne's view
Petrous pyramid
Lateral view
Sphenoid sinus

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Caldwell view is done for: [AIIMS 2011]
questions.explanation: "Lateral view is best for the sphenoid sinus." Caldwell view is the occipito frontal view. The frontal sinuses are seen clearly in this view.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: For viewing superior orbital fissure-best view is: [AIIMS 97]
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 434. Superior orbital fissure can be seen by Caldwell view and Water's view.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Complications of acute sinusitis: [PGI 03]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scotts Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1539, 1540; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 305.
Complications of Sinusitis—Acute Sinusitis
Local (due to local spread)
Systemic (due to hematogenous spread)
Frontal sinusitis can cause: Subperiosteal abscess/or Pott's puffy tumor, Osteomyelitis
Brain abscess (can occur as a result of local spread as well hematogenous spread secondary to maxillary sinusitis associated with dental disease)
Ethmoid sinusitis can cause: Orbital cellulitis
Meningitis
Toxic shock syndrome
The stages of orbital cellulitis are:
Preseptal cellulitis (infection anterior to orbital septum)
Postseptal cellulitis or orbital cellulitis without abscess (i.e. infection posterior to orbital septum)
Subperiosteal abscess (pus collects beneath the periosteum)
Orbital abscess (pus collects in orbit)
Cavernous sinus thrombosis/abscess (includes chemosis)
Maxillary sinusitis – no acute complications.
Sphenoid sinusitis can lead to: Cavernous sinus thrombosis, Intracranial complications.
NOTE:
Mucocele, Pyocele and pneumatocele are complications of Chronic Sinusitis.
If infection in the frontal sinus spreads to the marrow of frontal bone, localized osteomyelitis with bone destruction can result in a doughy swelling of forehead, classically called as 'Pott's Puffy Tumor'. Surgical drainage and debridement should be done in this case.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Complication of sinus disease include: [AIIMS 93]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Tuli 1/e, p 196; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1539, 1540; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 305.
As Discussed in Previous Question:
There is no confusion regarding orbital cellulitis, and cavernous sinus thrombosis being the complications of sinusitis.
Dhingra does not mention Retrobulbar neuritis as one of the complications of sinusitis but according to Tuli 1st/ed, p 196 posterior group of sinuses can lead to neuritis with impaired vision.
Complications of Posterior Group of Sinuses
Superior orbital fissure syndrome/orbital apex syndrome.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Neuritis with impaired vision.
Oroantral fistula/sublabial fistula.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Orbital cellulitis is a complication of: [MP 09]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1485; Parson Disease of Eye 20/e, p 457.
Orbital cellulitis can occur as a complication of sinusitis and injuries. As far as endoscopic sinus surgery is concerned, it can lead to orbital and intracranial complications so orbital cellulitis can occur in it also.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Angular vein infection commonly causes thrombosis of: [TN]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 201; TB of Mohan Bansal, p 307.
Angular vein which begins from medial angle of eye, continues as the facial vein. The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus through the deep facial vein and pterygoid plexus of veins.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: A patient with sinus infection develops chemosis, B/L proptosis and fever, the diagnosis goes in favor of: [PGI 99]
questions.explanation: B/L proptosis, fever and chemosis point towards cavernous sinus thrombosis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Most definitive diagnosis of sinusitis is: [AIIMS 92]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1442; Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 277; Turner 10/e, p 43.
According to Scott Brown's 7/e, Vol 2, p 1142: "There are many possible methods to make diagnosis of rhinosinusitis but there is much debate related to best method. It has become increasingly clear that the diagnosis of ABRS (acute bacterial rhinosinusitis) is best made on clinical grounds and criteria."
But this option is not given.
Scott Brown's further says: "At this time, a maxillary sinus tap with cultures, revealing pathogenic organism remains the gold standard for the diagnosis of ABRS, although there is increasing interest in the role of endoscopic-guided middle meatal cultures, in lieu of maxillary sinus tap. It has even been suggested that endoscopically guided cultures may be a preferred culture technique to maxillary sinus taps, as they can identify patients with ethmoid infection." Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1442.
Remember:
The 1st investigation to be done in chronic sinusitis is nasal endoscopy (to visualize the nasal mucosa, meatuses etc). If any pathology is found then NCCT of nose & PNS is done.
Best Investigation for chronic sinusitis – NCCT nose & PNS.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Pathognomonic feature of Maxillary sinusitis is: [UP 07]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 205.
Characteristic finding of maxillary sinusitis on Rhinoscopy is pus or mucopus in the middle meatus. Mucosa and turbinates may appear red and swollen.
Remember: Dental infections are an important source of maxillary sinusitis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Frontal mucocele presents as: [PGI 96]

options.text: Swelling above medial canthus, below the floor of frontal sinus
Swelling above eyebrow lateral to grabella

questions.answerText: Swelling above medial canthus, below the floor of frontal sinus
questions.explanation: Frontal sinus mucocele presents as a firm, non-tender swelling in superomedial quadrant of the orbit (above the medial canthus, below the floor of frontal sinus). Displacement of the eye ball—Forward, downward and lateral i.e, proptosis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Mucocele is commonly seen in sinus: [DNB 07]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 198; Tuli 1/e, p 196; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1531.
A mucocele is an epithelial lined, mucus containing sac completely filling the sinus and capable of expansion.
Mucocele are most commonly formed in Frontal sinus followed by ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary sinuses.
Mucocele of frontal sinus presents as a swelling in the floor of frontal sinus above the inner (medial) canthus. It displaces the eyeball forward, downward and laterally.
IOC = CT scanTOC = Endoscopic sinus surgery
According to Dhingra, 6th/ed p 198: Least common sinus associated with Mucocele formation is sphenoid.
But Scott Brown 7th/ed Vol 2 p 1531 says: Most of the cases of mucocele of sphenoid sinus are referred to neurosurgeons. Therefore, it seems it is less common but actually the sinus least involved by mucocele is maxilla.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Most common site for osteoma is: [MP 08]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1521.
Craniofacial osteomas are benign tumors often originating in the paranasal sinuses. The frontal sinus is the most frequent location followed by the ethmoid, maxillary and sphenoid sinus, respectively.
Age of presentation = second to fifth decade with a male-female ratio – 3:1.
Presentation:
Generally they are an incidental finding on radiography
It may produce symptoms like: Visual impairment, Intracranial neurological complications like meningitis or pneumocephalus with seizure.
Management: Removal by endoscopic sinus surgery.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: A 2-year-old child with purulent nasal discharge, fever and pain since 2 months. His fever is 102–103°C, and leucocyte count is 12000 cu/mm. X-ray PNS showed opacification of left ethmoidal air cells. The culture of the eye discharge was negative. Which of the following would be most useful further step in evaluation of this patient? [AI 10]

options.text: Repeat culture of the eye discharge

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 208-213.
The child is presenting with fever and purulent nasal discharge with X-ray PNS showing opacification of ethmoidal sinus, i.e. probably the child is having chronic sinusitis (as it is present for the past 2 months) with an acute exacerbation. Now the most dreaded complication of ethmoidal sinusitis is orbital complication.
"Orbital complication – most of the complications, follow infection of ethmoids as they are separated from the orbit only by a thin lamina of bone – lamina papyracea. Infection travels from these sinuses either by ostitis or a thrombophlebitic process of ethmoidal veins." Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 213.
The best method to assess the status of ethmoidal air cells and its complications is CT scan.
"CT is particularly useful in ethmoid and sphenoid sinus infections and has replaced studies with contrast material." Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 209.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: A 24-year-old female with long standing history of sinusitis present with fevers, headache (recent origin) and personality changes; Fundus examination revealed papilledema. Most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Read below.
Patient is presenting with fever, headache and personality changes which is typical of frontal lobe abscess (which is a complication of chronic sinusitis). In meningitis and encephalitis although patient presents with fever and headache, but personality changes are not seen.
Frontal bone osteomyelitis (Pott's puffy tumor) presents as doughy swelling on forehead.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Cavernous sinus thrombosis following sinusitis results in all of the following signs except: [PGI]

options.text: Constricted pupil in response to light
Engorgement of retinal veins upon ophthalmoscopic examination

questions.answerText: Constricted pupil in response to light
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 214.
Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia occur in cavernous sinus thrombosis due to involvement of III, IV and V cranial nerves. Retinal vessels are also engorged but pupils are fixed and dilated (not constricted), due to involvement of III nerve and sympathetic plexus.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: All are true about mucormycosis, except: [PGI]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Current Otolaryngology 3/e, p 295.
Mucormycosis is caused by Rhizopus species, Rhizomucus and Absidia species.
Initially, the disease runs a subtle course with only fever and rhinorrhea. Later on, it invades the orbit and intracranial cavity with rapid loss of vision, meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis and multiple cranial nerve palsies.
It has marked predilection for vascular invasion leading to widespread thrombosis, tissue necrosis, and gangrene.
Characteristic nasal finding is a dark necrotic turbinate surrounded by pale mucosa blackish discharge and crusts.
M/C site is middle turbinate followed by middle meatus and septum.
Investigation of choice is MRI, while biopsy is confirmatory.
Treatment: Includes amphotericin-B, heparin, hyperbaric oxygen, and debridement.
Mucormycosis is characterized by angioinvasion, aseptate hyphae, and is associated with deferoxamine therapy (not long-term, but deferoxamine therapy is a risk factor). It can lead to blindness.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: The best surgical treatment for chronic maxillary sinusitis is: [MP 02]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Current Otolaryngology 2/e, p 279, 280; Dhingra 5/e, p 205, 209.
Discussed in text. FESS is the current treatment of choice for chronic maxillary sinusitis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: FESS means: [Mahara 02]
questions.explanation: FESS means Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Endoscopic nasal surgery is indicated in: [Manipal 04]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 419; Head and Neck surgery, DeSouza, p 127; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1481.
Endoscopic nasal surgery is indicated in both chronic sinusitis and epistaxis.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20A: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinusitis
questions.stem: Indications of FESS: [PGI Nov 2010]
questions.explanation:
All of the above are indications of FESS.
Indications of Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS)
A. Nasal conditions:
Indian = Inflammation of sinus (sinusitis - chronic and fungal)
Prime = Polyp removal
Minister = Mucocele of frontal and ethmoid sinus
Can = Choanal atresia repair
Speak = Septoplasty
Fluent = Foreign body removal
English = Epistaxis
B. Other conditions:Nose is separated from orbit by lamina papyracea, anterior cranial fossa by cribriform plate and pituitary by sphenoid. Hence FESS can be used in:
Orbital conditions: Orbital decompression, Optic nerve decompression, Blow out of orbit, Drainage of periorbital abscess, Dacryocystorhinostomy
CSF leak
Pituitary surgery like trans sphenoid hypophysectomy
END OF CHAPTER 20A MCQs
Anatomy and Physiology of Paranasal Sinuses - Development, Maxillary (Antrum of Highmore, 1st to develop, Largest sinus, M/C bacterial sinusitis), Frontal (Last to develop, Pott's puffy tumor, Mucocele, Ivory osteoma), Ethmoidal (Well developed at birth, M/C sinusitis in children, Orbital cellulitis, Adenocarcinoma in wood workers), Sphenoidal (Not present at birth, Least common sinusitis, Cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis, Optic nerve/ICA relations)
Nerve Supply - Maxillary (V2), Frontal (V1), Ethmoidal (V1 + V2), Sphenoidal (V1 + V2)
Development Table - At birth, Adult size, Growth, Radiological appearance
Acute Sinusitis - >7 days, <4 weeks, M/C sinus in adults (Maxillary), M/C in children (Ethmoidal), Organisms (S. pneumoniae M/C, H. influenzae 2nd M/C, Moraxella), Clinical features (Major/Minor criteria), Maxillary/Frontal/Ethmoid/Sphenoid sinusitis symptoms, Diagnosis (Anterior rhinoscopy, CT scan), Radiological views (Water's, Caldwell's, Lateral, Basal), Treatment (Antibiotics, Decongestants, Analgesics, Steam inhalation)
Chronic Sinusitis - >12 weeks, Mixed aerobic/anaerobic, Maxillary M/C, Diagnosis (Nasal endoscopy 1st, NCCT), Treatment (Medical, Surgical: Antral lavage, Intranasal antrostomy, Caldwell-Luc, FESS, Trephination, External frontoethmoidectomy)
Fungal Sinusitis - Aspergillus (M/C), Types (Fungus ball, Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, Chronic invasive, Acute fulminant), Fungus ball (Maxillary > Sphenoid, FESS), AFRS (Dematiaceous species, Bent and Kuhn criteria), Mucormycosis (Uncontrolled diabetes, Black necrotic mass, Angioinvasion, Amphotericin B, Surgical debridement)
Complications of Sinusitis - Local (Mucocele, Osteomyelitis), Orbital (Preseptal cellulitis, Subperiosteal abscess, Orbital cellulitis, Orbital abscess, Superior orbital fissure syndrome), Intracranial (Meningitis M/C, Extradural abscess, Subdural abscess, Brain abscess, Cavernous sinus thrombosis), Descending infections
Orbital Complications - M/C complication, Ethmoiditis, Preseptal/Postseptal cellulitis, Subperiosteal abscess, Orbital abscess, Superior orbital fissure syndrome, Orbital apex syndrome
Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis - Ethmoid/sphenoid sinusitis, B/L involvement, VI nerve first, Pupils dilated and fixed, Treatment (Antibiotics 4-6 weeks, Drainage)
Osteomyelitis - Frontal bone (M/C, Diploic bone, Pott's puffy tumor), Maxilla (Infants/children)
Mucocele/Pyocele - Epithelial-lined mucus-containing sac, Frontal > Ethmoid > Sphenoid > Maxillary, Frontal mucocele (Superomedial quadrant of orbit, Proptosis), Treatment (Radical frontoethmoidectomy, Endoscopic)
FESS - Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery, Messerklinger's technique (Anterior to posterior: Uncinectomy → Anterior ethmoidectomy → Posterior ethmoidectomy → Middle meatal antrostomy), Wigand's technique (Posterior to anterior), Indications (Nasal: Sinusitis, Polyps, Mucocele, Choanal atresia, Septoplasty, Foreign body, Epistaxis; Others: Orbital decompression, Optic nerve decompression, DCR, CSF leak, Pituitary surgery), Complications (Orbital, Intracranial, Carotid artery injury - most feared, Optic nerve injury - posterior ethmoid/sphenoid)
Caldwell-Luc Surgery - Sublabial incision through canine fossa, Nasoantral window in inferior meatus, Indications (Foreign body, Dental cyst, Oroantral fistula, Fractures, Approach to pterygopalatine fossa), Contraindication (Malignancy maxilla - spreads to cheek), M/C complication (Facial swelling, Infraorbital nerve injury 2nd M/C), Instruments (Tilley's harpoon, Tilley's antral burr, Luc's forceps, Krause nasal snare)

questions.stem: M/C site of osteomas among paranasal sinuses is:
questions.explanation:
Ref. TB of ENT, Hazarika 3/e, P 370. See text for explanation.
Osteoma is the most common benign slow growing tumor of paranasal sinus. Most common sinus involved is Frontal > Ethmoids > Maxillary sinus.

questions.stem: M/C site for fibrous dysplasia is:
questions.explanation: Ref. TB of ENT, Hazarika 3/e, P 371. M/C bone involved is maxilla. The fibrous tissue can expand to fill the maxillary sinus also.

questions.chapter: Chapter 20B: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinonasal Tumor
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20B: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinonasal Tumor · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Ohngren's classification of maxillary sinus carcinoma is based on:

options.text: Imaginary plane between the medical canthus of eye and angle of mandible
Imaginary plane between lateral canthus of eye and angle of mandible
Two horizontal lines, one passing through floor of orbit and other through floor of antrum

questions.answerText: Imaginary plane between the medical canthus of eye and angle of mandible
questions.explanation: See text for explanation. Ohngren's line is an imaginary line which extends between medial canthus and the angle of mandible, divides the maxilla into two regions anteroinferior and posterosuperior. Anteroinferior growths are easy to manage and have better prognosis than posterosuperior tumors.

questions.chapter: Chapter 20B: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinonasal Tumor
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20B: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinonasal Tumor · New-pattern question
questions.stem: First lymph node involved in maxillary carcinoma:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 207.
In paranasal sinus tumors:
Lymphatic spread: Nodal metastases are uncommon and occur only in the late stages of disease. Submandibular and upper jugular nodes are enlarged. Maxillary and ethmoid sinuses drain primarily into retropharyngeal nodes, but these nodes are inaccessible to palpation.
Systemic metastases are rare. May be seen in the lungs (most commonly) and occasionally in bone.
Intracranial spread can occur through ethmoids, cribriform plate or foramen lacerum.

questions.chapter: Chapter 20B: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinonasal Tumor
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20B: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinonasal Tumor · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Tumor arising from olfactory nasal mucosa:
questions.explanation: Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 204. Also called as olfactory placode tumor as it arises from olfactory epithelium in the upper third of nose. Bimodal peak of incidence at 10-20 and 50-60 years.

questions.explanation: Inverted papilloma arises from the lateral nasal wall in middle meatus rarely on the septum.

questions.chapter: Chapter 20B: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinonasal Tumor
questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 20B: Diseases of Paranasal Sinus—Sinonasal Tumor
questions.stem: Inverted papilloma: [PGI 02; PGI Nov 09]
questions.explanation:
Inverted papilloma:
Age: 40-70 years (adults)
Sex: Male > Female
Site: Lateral nasal wall in middle meatus
Associated with HPV
Features: Finger-like epithelial invasions into underlying stroma, Usually unilateral, Locally aggressive, U/L nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, U/L epistaxis, In 10-15% cases associated with squamous cell carcinoma (premalignant)
Treatment: Maxillectomy (Lateral rhinotomy or sublabial degloving approach; Endoscopic approach preferred)
Tendency to recur after surgical removal (as it is multicentric)

questions.stem: True about basal cell carcinoma: [PGI 04]

questions.explanation:
Ref. Current Otolaryngology 3/e, p 238, 239; Scott Brown 7/e, Vol 2, p 1705, 1706.
Read the preceding text for explanation.
Basal Cell Carcinoma
Usually seen in middle age and above (40-80 years)
M/C in Males
Main etiology is UV exposure
Usually seen above a line joining angle of mouth and ear lobule
Commonest site is inner canthus of eye
Commonest variety is Nodular (painless shiny nodule)
Locally infiltrating tumor, may erode surrounding tissue (Rodent ulcer)
No lymphatic/bloodstream spread (Rarely metastasize)
Diagnostic procedure of choice: Wedge biopsy
Treatment of choice: Wide surgical excision
Chemotherapy: Topical 5% imiquimod, topical 5 fluorouracil
In patients > 60 years: Radiotherapy is the treatment

questions.stem: Which of the following nasal tumors originates from the olfactory mucosa? [AI 12]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 6/e, p 204; Current Otolaryngology 3/e, p 313.
Esthesioneuroblastoma (ENB), also known as olfactory neuroblastoma, is a rare neoplasm originating from olfactory neuroepithelium superior to middle turbinate. They are initially unilateral and can grow into the adjacent sinuses, contralateral nasal cavity and they can spread to orbit and brain. It can cause paraneoplastic syndrome by secreting vasoactive peptides. Since it can spread intracranially craniofacial resection is the surgery of choice. Combination therapy (Surgery + RT + CT) is used in management.
NOTE: Contrary to other nasal malignancies it is M/C in females.

questions.stem: Ground glass appearance of maxillary sinus on CT scan is seen on: [DPG 2007]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Internet search. Fibrous dysplasia shows ground glass appearance on CT scan.
END OF CHAPTER 20B MCQs
Predisposing Factors - Nickel (Squamous cell/Anaplastic carcinoma), Hardwood/Softwood (Adenocarcinoma of ethmoidal sinus), Hydrocarbons, Mustard gas, Radium dial workers (Soft tissue sarcoma), Welding/soldering, Age (5th decade), Sex (M:F = 2:1)
Points to Remember - M/C malignancy of nasal skin (Basal cell carcinoma), M/C benign tumor of nose (Capillary hemangioma), M/C benign tumor of PNS (Osteoma, M/C site frontal sinus), M/C malignant tumor of nose and PNS (Squamous cell carcinoma)
Papilloma - Skin of nasal vestibule and anterior septum, Cautery/cryotherapy
Inverted Papilloma/Transitional Cell Papilloma/Schneiderian Papilloma/Ringertz Tumor - Age 40-70 years, Male > Female, Lateral nasal wall in middle meatus, HPV associated, Finger-like epithelial invasions, U/L, Locally aggressive, Premalignant (10-15% associated with SCC), Treatment (Maxillectomy - Lateral rhinotomy/sublabial degloving/endoscopic), Tendency to recur
Malignant Tumors of Nose - Squamous cell carcinoma (M/C, Nose pickers cancer, Lateral wall, Men >50 years, RT + Surgery), Malignant Melanoma (Bluish-black polypoidal mass, Anterior part of nasal septum, Wide surgical excision), Olfactory Neuroblastoma/Esthesioneuroblastoma (Neuroendocrine tumor, Bimodal age peaks 11-20 and 50-60 years, M/C in females, Upper third of nasal cavity, Craniofacial resection), Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (Antrum and Nose, Swiss-cheese pattern, Perineural spread), Basal Cell Carcinoma (Middle age and above, M/C in Males, UV exposure, Inner canthus, Nodular variety, Rodent ulcer, No lymphatic/bloodstream spread, Wedge biopsy, Wide surgical excision, Mohs surgery)
Paranasal Sinus Tumors - Benign (Osteoma - M/C benign, Frontal > Ethmoids > Maxillary, Ground glass appearance, Excision; Fibrous Dysplasia - 5-15 years, M/C in females, Maxilla > Mandible, Canine fossa/zygomatic area, Ground glass appearance, Surgery, McCune-Albright syndrome)
Malignant Tumors of PNS - Etiology (Hardwood - Adenocarcinoma, Nickel - SCC/Anaplastic, Leather industry, Mustard gas), Histology (80% SCC, Adenocarcinoma, Adenoid cystic carcinoma, Melanoma, Sarcomas), Site (Maxillary antrum M/C), Age (7th decade), Sex (Male > Female), Symptoms (Early: Nasal stuffiness, U/L Epistaxis, Facial paraesthesia/pain, Epiphora, Dental pain; Late: Spread to medial/anterior/inferior/superior/posterior), Lymphatic spread (Nodal metastases uncommon, Retropharyngeal LN earliest, Submandibular LN commonest), Diagnosis (Biopsy, CECT best investigation), Classification (Ohngren's - imaginary plane between medial canthus and angle of mandible; Lederman's - Suprastructure/Mesostructure/Infrastructure), Treatment (Surgery + Radiotherapy, Total/Partial maxillectomy, Weber-Ferguson incision, Craniofacial resection, Barbosa technique for infratemporal extension), Prognosis (5 year cure rate 30%), Ethmoid sinus malignancy (Poor prognosis)

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 21: Oral Cavity · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Grayish white membrane in throat may be seen in all of the following infections except:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 274; Harrison 17/e, p 210; Mohan Bansal p 544.
Membrane in Throat is Caused by
Pyogenic organisms viz. Streptococci, Staphylococci causing membranous tonsillitis
Diphtheria
Vincent's angina (Caused by fusiform bacilli and spirochetes: Borrelia vincentii)
Candidiasis/monoliasis/oral thrush —Maqbool 11th/ed p 280
Infectious mononucleosis
Agranulocytosis
Leukemia
Aphthous ulcers
Traumatic ulcers
From the above list it is clear that streptococcus (option 'a') and diphtheria (option 'b') causes membrane over throat.
This leaves us with 2 options—Adenovirus and Ludwig's angina.
Harrison 17th/ed, p 210 says about Adenovirus pharyngitis: "Since pharyngeal exudate may be present on examination, this condition is difficult to differentiate from streptococcal pharyngitis."
So adenovirus may also be associated with membrane in throat but Ludwig's angina is infection of the submandibular space and never presents with membrane over the tonsil/throat.
So amongst the given options—Ludwig's angina is the best option.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 21: Oral Cavity · New-pattern question
questions.stem: Black color patch in the mouth is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Ref. Logan Turner 10/e, p 87, 88.
Vincent's Angina (Ulcerative Gingivitis/Trench mouth):
Was common during first world war (due to lack of oral hygiene) and is less common now.
Caused by fusiform bacillus and spirochetes: Borrelia vincentii.
It manifests as necrotizing gingivostomatitis with oropharyngeal ulcerations and dark gray membrane.
O/E:
Membrane generally present on one tonsil but may involve the gum, soft and hard palate.
It appears as grayish black slough which bleeds when it is removed.
Ulcers are visible on tonsil after removal of membrane.
Membrane reforms after removal.
Characteristic smell in breath (halitosis), so also called as Trench mouth.
Treatment:
Systemic antibiotics: Penicillin, Erythromycin, Metronidazole.
Warm sodium bicarbonate gargles.
Barrier nursing of the patient as disease is infectious.

options.text: Firmly attached and bleeds on removal

questions.answerText: Firmly attached and bleeds on removal
questions.explanation:

In diphtheria: membrane is dirty grey in color.

It is adherent and its removal leaves a bleeding surface.
Cervical lymph nodes particularly the jugulodigastric lymph node are enlarged and become tender, giving a bull neck appearance.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 21: Oral Cavity
questions.stem: Fordyce's (Spots) Granules in oral cavity arise from: [AIIMS 04]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Scott Brown's Otolaryngology 7/e, vol 2, p 1824; Harrison 17/e, p 128; Dhingra 5/e, p 205, 6/e, p 220; Turner 10/e, p 233; Mohan Bansal p 379.
Fordyce's Spot:
Yellowish lesions seen in buccal and labial mucosa.
They are ectopic sebaceous glands and do not have any erythematous halo.
Seen in upto 80% of population.
No clinical significance.
Points to Remember
Forchheimer spots: seen in rubella, infectious mononucleosis and scarlet fever.
Rothe's spots: seen in Infective endocarditis
Rose spots: seen in Typhoid fever
Koplik's spot: seen in Measles (above the second molar).

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 21: Oral Cavity
questions.stem: True about aphthous ulcer: [PGI June 05]

options.text: Involves the mucosa of the hard palate

questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 230, 6/e, p 218; Mohan Bansal p 381-2.
Aphthous ulcers are recurrent and superficial ulcers, usually involving movable mucosa i.e. inner surfaces of lips, buccal mucosa, tongue, floor of mouth and soft palate, while sparing mucosa of the hard palate and gingivae.
Etiology
Is unknown but may be due to:
Nutritional deficiency of vit. B12, folic acid and iron.
Viral infection
Hormonal changes
Treatment
Topical steroids and cauterization with 10% silver nitrate
Points to Remember
Recurrence is common in ulcers.
M/C cause of viral oral ulcer = Herpes simplex type I
Painless oral ulcers are seen in—syphilis
Behcet's syndrome is oral ulcers + genital ulcers + eye disease (iridocyclitis and retinal vasculitis) + vascular malformation.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 21: Oral Cavity
questions.stem: True regarding Ranula: [AI 01]

options.text: It is also called as epulis
It is a cystic swelling in the floor of mouth.
It is a type of thyroglossal cyst
It is a type of mucus retention cyst

questions.answerText: It is a cystic swelling in the floor of mouth.
questions.explanation:
Ref. Dhingra 5/e, p 237, 6/e, p 224; Surgical Short Cases 3/e, p 45, 46; Mohan Bansal p 403.
Ranula:
It is a thin walled bluish retention cyst.
Seen in the floor of mouth on one side of the frenulum.
It arises due to obstruction of duct of sublingual salivary gland.
It is almost always unilateral.
Clinical Features:
Seen mostly in children and young adults.
Only complaint—swelling in the floor of mouth.
Cyst may rupture spontaneously but recurrence is common.
O/E:
Bluish in color - Brilliantly translucent
Lymph nodes are not enlarged
Types:
Simple: Situated in floor of mouth without any cervical prolongation.
Deep/Plunging: Ranula which extends to the neck through the muscles of mylohyoid. Such prolongation appears in submandibular region.
Management:
Surgical excision of ranula along with sublingual salivary gland is the ideal treatment.
M/C D/D of ranula = sublingual dermoid (opaque midline swelling)
During excision of ranula = M/C nerve which can be damaged is lingual nerve.
NOTE:
Cavernous ranula is a type of lymphangioma which invades the fascial planes of neck.
Obstruction of duct of sublingual salivary gland leads to ranula formation but obstruction of parotid and submandibular gland duct leads to their atrophy. This is because sublingual gland is active throughout whereas parotid and submandibular gland secret saliva only in response to food.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 21: Oral Cavity
questions.stem: Which of the following is premalignant condition: [AIIMS 91]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Devita 7/e, p 982; Bailey and Love 25/e, p 735.
Lesions and conditions of the oral mucosa associated with an increased risk of malignancy
Premalignant conditions
Conditions increasing risk
Risk is doubtful
Leukoplakia, Erythroplakia, Speckled erythroplakia, Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis
Oral submucosa fibrosis, Syphilitic glossitis, Sideropenic dysphagia (Paterson-Kelly syndrome)
Oral lichen planus, Discoid lupus erythematosus, Dyskeratosis congenita
NOTE:
Premalignant lesion is morphologically altered tissue where cancer is more likely to occur e.g. Leukoplakia whereas premalignant condition is a generalised state where there is significantly increased risk of cancer, e.g. syphilis, submucous fibrosis.
Plummer Vinson syndrome can lead to post cricoid carcinoma (M/C), carcinoma of tongue, oesophagus and stomach.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 21: Oral Cavity
questions.stem: The most common premalignant condition of oral carcinoma is: [AI 95, 96]
questions.explanation:
Ref. Devita 7/e, p 982; Bailey and Love 25/e, p 735; Mohan Bansal p 376-7.
"Leukoplakia is the most common premalignant oral mucosal lesion." Mohan Bansal p 377.
"The malignant potential of erythroplakia is 17 times higher than in leukoplakia." Mohan Bansal p 376.
Points to Remember
Most common premalignant condition for oral cancer: Leukoplakia or speckled leukoplakia
Premalignant condition with highest risk for oral cancer: Erythroplakia. (M/C Site = lower alveolar margin and floor of mouth)
Painless oral ulcers are seen in–syphilis
Behcet's syndrome = oral ulcers + genital ulcers + eye disease (iridocyclitis and retinal vasculitis) + vascular malformation.
Important Points on Leukoplakia
Clinical white patch that can't be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease is leukoplakia.
Most common site is buccal mucosa and oral commissures.
Tobacco smoking and chewing are main etiological factor.
If patient stops smoking for 1 year, it will disappear in 60% of cases.
Features suggestive malignant change in leukoplakia are induration, speckled or nodular appearance.
Chances of malignant changes in leukoplakia increases with increases in age of lesion and age of patient.
All lesions must be biopsied and sent for histology as it has 2-8% risk of malignancy.
Lesion
Treatment
Hyperkeratosis
Follow-up at 4 monthly interval/chemopreventive drugs
Dysplasia
Surgical excision or CO2 laser excision
Remember: Chemopreventive drugs used in oral malignancy: Vit. A, E, C, Betacarotene, Flavonoids, Celecoxib.

questions.src: Self Assessment & Review ENT, Sakshi Arora Hans 7/e · Chapter 21: Oral Cavity
questions.stem: The most common site of oral cancer among Indian population is: [AI 04]
questions.explanation:
Ref. ASI 1st/ed p 348; Oncology and Surgery Journal 2004 p 161.
Frequency of various cancer of oral cavity in India are:
Buccal mucosa 38%
Anterior tongue 16%
Lower alveolus, floor of mouth 15%
So, most common site of oral cancer among Indian population is buccal mucosa or in this question alveobuccal complex (due to their predilection for pan chewing where tobacco is kept in lower gingivobuccal sulcus).
Remember:
Most common site of oral cancer in world: Tongue
Most common histological variety of oral cancer: Squamous cell carcinoma
M/C histological variety of lip carcinoma – squamous cell carcinoma
M/C histological variety of upper lip carcinoma – Basal cell carcinoma
Oral malignancy with best prognosis = lip cancer
M/C site for Ca lip = lower lip
Oral malignancy with worst prognosis = floor of mouth.
